findings.headline: Employee retention remains above target at 90%, indicating staff stability despite organisational change
findings.detail: Employee retention stands at 90%, above the 87% target, maintained through Retention Advisor and Assistant roles, leavers discussions, and service-based listening sessions. The council acknowledges ongoing uncertainty about organisational change but credits direct engagement activity with sustaining retention.
findings.matters: Retaining staff maintains service continuity and avoids costly recruitment and training; stable retention above target despite announced organisational change is a positive signal that people management and change communication are working effectively.
findings.figures: 90.00% retention rate (target: 87%); employee turnover 9.90% (within target range 10-13%)
findings.quote: Retention remains above the target of 87%. All leavers continue to be offered a leavers discussion or to complete the online tool, helping to inform retention policy.

findings.headline: Subject Access Requests increased 18% year-on-year in Q1, though performance remained at target
findings.detail: The council received over 130 Subject Access Requests (SARs) in Q1 2026/27, which is 18% more than the same quarter in the previous year. The council achieved 90% compliance with the one-month statutory deadline, meeting the target. The council is working with specific services and holding weekly meetings to maintain timeliness.
findings.matters: Significant year-on-year increase in data access requests could signal growing demand for data handling services or potential compliance scrutiny; sustained demand growth at this rate may require additional resource investment to maintain performance.
findings.figures: 130+ SARs received Q1 2026/27, 18% more than Q1 2025/26; 90% met statutory deadline (target: 90%)
findings.quote: There continue to be high levels of requests, with over 130 received in the first quarter which is 18% more than in the first quarter of 25/26.

findings.headline: 27% of customer complaint responses were overdue in Q1 2026/27 in new baseline reporting
findings.detail: The council is reporting on complaint response timeliness for the first time under new feedback management arrangements. In Q1 2026/27, 27% of complaints received were overdue—either no response by deadline or response after deadline. The council acknowledges this establishes a baseline and will monitor through future quarters to identify trends and emerging themes.
findings.matters: A quarter of complaints not meeting the response deadline suggests potential resource constraints in complaint handling or reflects broader operational stress; unresolved complaint backlogs can indicate underlying service quality issues requiring financial investment.
findings.figures: 27% of complaints received in Q1 2026/27 were overdue (new baseline measure)
findings.quote: Quarter 1 represents the first reporting period for this indicator under the Council's enhanced feedback management arrangements and should therefore be regarded as establishing a baseline position. The figure shown represents the total position for the Council as a whole.

findings.headline: Long-term sickness absence higher in 2026 than 2025 despite overall decline in absence days
findings.detail: The council reports that while total FTE days lost due to sickness absence continues to decline gradually, the proportion of the workforce taking long-term sickness absence (over 21 days) has been higher in 2026 than 2025. Mental health-related absence and stress remain the top two reasons for long-term absence. The council has implemented wellbeing interventions including Mental Health First Aid training, occupational health services, and targeted support for PTSD.
findings.matters: Long-term sickness has direct financial implications through occupational health costs, sick pay, and need for replacement staffing; rising long-term absence despite falling overall absence rates signals underlying wellbeing issues that could worsen if unaddressed and increase future costs.
findings.figures: 12-month rolling average: 8.51 days per FTE (within target range 8-10 days); 54% of new HR cases April-June 2026 were absence/health related, of which 55% were long-term absence
findings.quote: While the proportion of the workforce recording sickness absence overall has reduced, the percentage taking long-term sickness absence has been higher in 2026 than 2025. It is therefore important to keep a continued focus on early support during absences and anything that can prevent those absences extending over 21 days.

findings.headline: Children in care fell to 50.4 per 10,000 from 53.4, meeting 51 per 10,000 target and moving from AMBER to GREEN.
findings.detail: The number of children in care per 10,000 population under 18 fell to 50.4 in March 2026 from 53.4 a year earlier, achieving the 51 per 10,000 target. This GREEN-rated indicator moved from AMBER status and shows a sustained downward trend (53.4 → 50.4 over 12 months). Alongside this, the number of children subject to child protection plans fell from 31.4 to 22.9 per 10,000. These improvements suggest both reduced incidence of need and more effective early intervention or prevention.
findings.matters: A council reducing both its in-care population and child protection caseloads demonstrates preventative capability and sustainable service management. This trend improves cost outlook for children's services and signals improving family support outcomes.
findings.figures: Children in care: 50.4 vs 53.4 per 10,000; Child protection plans: 22.9 vs 31.4 per 10,000
findings.quote: Of the six indicators with comparable previous results, three (50%) improved, while three (50%) declined...CYP 001 - The number of children in care per 10,000 population under 18...CYP 003 - Number of Children subject to child protection plan...Amber to Green

findings.headline: Independent Domestic Violence Advocacy service engagement improved from 55% to 77%, exceeding 70% target and moving from RED to GREEN.
findings.detail: The percentage of clients engaging with the council's IDVA service increased to 77% in Q4 2025/26 from 55% a year earlier, exceeding the 70% target. This GREEN-rated indicator moved from RED status in 2024/25, representing an 22-percentage-point improvement and successful service development. The quarterly data shows sustained improvement (55% → 71% → 81% → 81% → 77%), indicating reliable delivery rather than a one-off result.
findings.matters: A council delivering measurable improvements in service engagement and quality provides reassurance to lenders about management capability and service sustainability. This is one of the few headline improvements across the report.
findings.figures: 77% current vs 55% previous vs 70% target
findings.quote: The percentage of clients engaging with Independent Domestic Violence Advocacy (IDVA) Service [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 77% 55% [Target] 70%

findings.headline: Municipal waste sent to landfill fell to 34.8% from 42.3%, and recycling rate increased to 58.6% from 53.3%.
findings.detail: The council achieved a 12-month rolling average of 34.8% of municipal waste being landfilled in Q4 2025/26, down from 42.3% a year earlier. Over the same period, the combined recycling, reuse, composting and recovery rate increased to 58.6% from 53.3%. Five of six Environment and Waste indicators improved compared to the previous year. These contextual (non-rated) indicators track progress toward the council's net-zero and climate change targets and show consistent positive direction of travel.
findings.matters: Environmental performance matters to councils' credit ratings and borrowing costs as ESG factors gain weight in investment decision-making. Consistent improvement on waste and carbon also signals operational discipline and strategic progress against declared targets.
findings.figures: Municipal waste landfilled: 34.8% vs 42.3% previous; Recycling rate: 58.6% vs 53.3% previous
findings.quote: the combined recycling, reuse, composting and recovery rate increased from 53.3% to 58.6%, while the proportion of municipal waste sent to landfill fell from 42.3% to 34.8%

findings.headline: Deaths registered within 5 days fell to 71% from 85%, missing 90% target.
findings.detail: The council registered 71% of deaths within 5 working days in Q4 2025/26, down from 85% a year earlier, against a 90% target. This RED-rated indicator represents a 14-percentage-point decline and regulatory non-compliance. The quarterly data shows volatility (85% → 85% → 56% → 93% → 84% → 71%), suggesting inconsistent service delivery in the registration service.
findings.matters: Death registration is a statutory function with specific timescales. Falling compliance represents regulatory failure and exposes the council to audit and inspection concern, while also affecting bereaved families' access to essential services.
findings.figures: 71% vs 85% previous vs 90% target
findings.quote: Registrations - All deaths registered within 5 days [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 71% 85% [Target] 90%

findings.headline: Child placement stability in the care system fell to 62.6% from 68.6%, remaining 12% below 71% target.
findings.detail: The percentage of child looked after placements lasting longer than 2 years for children in care for more than 2.5 years fell to 62.6% in March 2026 from 68.6% a year earlier, against a target of 71%. The monthly data shows steady decline from 68.6% in March 2025 through to 62.6% by March 2026, with an accelerated drop from January 2026 onward (68.2% → 63.8% → 62.6%). This RED-rated indicator reflects reduced stability in placements and signals both quality outcomes risk and potential cost pressure from higher placement churn.
findings.matters: Placement instability in care is costly—each move is an intervention and often to more expensive provision. A council unable to maintain placement stability for children faces both quality and budget risk.
findings.figures: 62.6% vs 68.6% previous vs 71% target
findings.quote: Placement Stability: Percentage of Child Looked After (CLA) placements longer than 2 years for Children being looked after for more than 2.5 years [March 2026 – March 2025] 62.6% 68.6% [Target] 71%

findings.headline: NHS Health Checks achievement fell to 52% from 71%, missing 67.5% target.
findings.detail: The council completed 52% of NHS Health Checks against the 67.5% target in Q4 2025/26, down from 71% in the same quarter a year earlier. This RED-rated indicator represents a 19-percentage-point decline in a year. The report does not explain the cause, but the sustained gap below target suggests a service under pressure or reaching capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Health Checks are a preventative public health intervention. Falling uptake signals either reduced service capacity or declining take-up, either of which represents missed prevention opportunity and potential future acute health cost growth.
findings.figures: 52% vs 71% previous vs 67.5% target
findings.quote: Achievement against target for completed NHS Health Checks [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 52% 71% [Target] 67.5%

findings.headline: EHCP assessments completed within 20 weeks improved to 11.7% from 6.9% but remain 42% below statutory target.
findings.detail: The council completed 11.7% of Education, Health and Care Plan assessments within the 20-week statutory timeframe in Q4 2025/26, up from 6.9% in the same quarter a year earlier. However, the target is 20%, placing the council significantly below statutory expectation. The quarterly data shows volatility, peaking at 23.6% in December 2025 before falling to 11.7% by March, suggesting bursts of activity followed by backlog growth.
findings.matters: Statutory deadlines for EHCP assessments are non-negotiable; miss them and the council faces legal challenge and remedial costs. This RED-rated indicator shows the council cannot sustain compliance with a core statutory duty, signalling either insufficient resource or systemic process failure.
findings.figures: 11.7% current vs 6.9% previous vs 20% target; peaked at 23.6% in December 2025
findings.quote: Percentage of Education Health and Care Plans (EHCP) completed within 20-week timeframe [March 2026 – March 2025] 11.7% 6.9% [Target] 20%

findings.headline: Contract waivers submitted less than 5 days before start date tripled to 26% from 7.2%, now RED rated.
findings.detail: The proportion of procurement waivers submitted on short notice (less than 5 days before their proposed start date) rose to 26% in Q4 2025/26 from 7.2% a year earlier, against a target of 20%. The report shows a consistent quarterly climb: 7.2% → 22% → 19% → 21% → 26%. This 26-percentage-point increase indicates stressed procurement processes and suggests the council is increasingly unable to plan purchases according to normal timescales.
findings.matters: A lender views short-notice contract waivers as evidence of process breakdown and loss of control. Short-notice waivers often precede emergency spending, may exclude competitive tendering, and signal operational pressure that can spread to other budget areas.
findings.figures: 26.0% vs 7.2% previous year; target 20%
findings.quote: Percentage of contract waivers submitted less than 5 days before their proposed start date [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 26.0% 7.2% [Target] 20%

findings.headline: Care home admissions for adults aged 18–64 remain 40% above target despite improving from 11.7 to 10.5 per 100,000.
findings.detail: Admissions of working-age adults to care homes are 10.5 per 100,000 population year-to-date, against a target of 7.5. While this represents improvement from 11.7 in the previous year, the council remains significantly above target. This RED-rated indicator reflects sustained pressure on the cost of care placements for younger adults.
findings.matters: Care home admissions are a high-cost driver in adult social care budgets. A council unable to meet a target it has set signals potential sustained overspend or limits on preventative and community support services.
findings.figures: 10.5 per 100,000 current vs 11.7 previous vs target 7.5 per 100,000
findings.quote: Long term support needs of adults (18-64) met by admission to residential and nursing care homes per 100,000 population (YTD) [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 10.5 [Previous] 11.7 [Target] 7.5

findings.headline: Highways Category 1 and 2 defect repair performance fell to 55% from 94%, now RED rated.
findings.detail: The council repaired 55% of Category 1 and 2 highway defects within operating standards in Q4 2025/26, down from 94% in Q4 2024/25. The report shows a steep decline beginning October 2025, falling from 95% to 55% by March 2026. This 39-percentage-point drop suggests operational capacity constraints in the highways maintenance service and represents the most significant deterioration across all measured indicators.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's ability to fund and deliver essential infrastructure maintenance must understand why a core service has lost two-thirds of its performance in six months, and what this implies for future maintenance backlogs and costs.
findings.figures: 55% vs 94% previous year; target 90%; monthly decline from 95% (April 2025) to 55% (March 2026)
findings.quote: Percentage of Category 1 & Category 2 defects repaired in line with Highways Operating Standards [Q4 2025/26 – Q4 2024/25] 55% [Previous] 94% [Target] 90%

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Streetlighting energy savings totalling £1.972m (21% underspend) have been delivered through LED replacement project, with year-to-date consumption approximately 50% of prior year.
findings.detail: The ongoing LED lantern replacement project is generating material energy savings. Year-to-date usage is approximately half that of the same period in the prior year, with further smaller reductions expected as the rollout continues. Additional underspend has emerged from annual electricity charge adjustment recalculation, PFI pension reconciliation, and maintenance savings linked to the LED project.
findings.matters: A lender should note evidence of successful cost management and efficiency delivery in one area, providing some offset to pressure areas, and indicating that energy infrastructure investment is delivering expected returns.
findings.figures: Streetlighting underspend £1.972m (21%), year-to-date usage 50% of prior year
findings.quote: Savings on streetlighting reflect reduced energy consumption from the ongoing LED lantern replacement project. Year to date usage is approximately half that of the same period in the prior year.

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: The council's DSG government grant submission was rejected in September 2026, with resubmission planned for October and no guarantee of receipt timing or funding for the £159.8m accumulated deficit.
findings.detail: In February 2026, government announced it would fund up to 90% of historical DSG deficits up to end 2025-26, conditional on submission of a recovery plan. Cambridgeshire submitted its plan in June 2026 after stakeholder engagement, received positive feedback from Department for Education advisors, but the submission was not accepted by government. Government has requested further information, and resubmission is planned for October 2026. No confirmation has been given on funding timing or whether the remaining 10% will be the council's liability.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on whether the £159.8m deficit will be funded externally or represent a long-term cash drain, as this affects both borrowing requirement and reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Up to 90% of historical deficits to be funded (subject to plan acceptance), 2026-27 deficit £63.3m, cumulative £159.8m
findings.quote: The Council submitted its plan to government in June 2026, following engagement with members and key stakeholders including the Integrated Care Board. The draft submission had received positive feedback from Department for Education advisors, but nevertheless was not accepted by government. Further information has been requested by government and a resubmission will be made in October.

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Adult social care debt collection is slipping, with overdue debt at £22.1m against a target of £21.8m and collection rate at 74% against a target of 77%.
findings.detail: The council's year-to-date collection performance on adult social care income is 74%, short of the 77% target. Overdue debt (91+ days) stands at £22.1m, marginally above the £21.8m target. The report attributes this to raised levels of billing from care contributions (£6m higher than forecast) and a backlog in financial assessments. Sundry debt has improved to £7.7m from higher levels following receipt of NHS Integrated Care Board income.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on whether the council can collect the income it depends on for adult social care funding, and whether poor collection is a cash-flow or bad-debt risk.
findings.figures: Collection rate 74% vs 77% target, ASC overdue debt £22.1m vs £21.8m target, billing £6m higher than forecast
findings.quote: Raised levels of adult social care debt remains common across councils. The Council is continuing to implement improvements to its debt recovery activities to ensure that the improvements seen last year and the flattening of an upward trend of overdue debt are maintained.

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Adult social care services are forecast to underspend by £3.927m (1.5%) of budget, providing partial offset to children's pressures but with volatility risk from demand and debt collection.
findings.detail: The Adults directorate opened with a £993k surplus from care budget realignment, benefiting from lower than expected demand in older people, mental health and learning disabilities budgets, and over-recovery against vacancy factor targets. However, emerging pressures in Physical Disabilities (£1.1m) and Older People income (£602k under-recovery from client contributions) are being reported, and adult social care debt remains elevated at £22.1m (91+ days overdue), creating income volatility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the adult services underspend is sustainable through the year given demand volatility, and whether overdue debt trends are manageable or indicate collection breakdown.
findings.figures: £3.927m underspend (1.5% of budget), £993k opening surplus, £1.1m Physical Disabilities pressure, £602k Older People income pressure, ASC debt £22.1m
findings.quote: The forecast position for Adults, Health and Commissioning budgets for the 2026-27 financial year as at the end of August 2026 is an underspend of £3,927k (equivalent to 1.5% of the annual budget).

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Children's external placements and home to school transport are together projecting an overspend of nearly £10m, driven by complexity of need in a small cohort and shortage of local provision.
findings.detail: Placements overspend is forecast at £6.658m, driven primarily by demand for high-cost residential placements for children with complex needs. Despite Cambridgeshire having a below-national rate of children in care (and declining numbers over the past six months), the unit cost of placements has risen sharply. Home to school transport is overspent by £2.236m, driven by rising numbers eligible for support (linked to EHCPs), increased complexity requiring specialist vehicles, and inflationary pressures in the transport market. Together these pressures are partly offset by other directorate underspends.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether children's services demand is structural (rising complexity despite declining numbers) and therefore resistant to normal cost-control measures, which would affect medium-term budget sustainability.
findings.figures: Placements overspend £6.658m, home to school transport overspend £2.236m (combined £8.894m), total two-area combined pressure 'nearly £10m'
findings.quote: The most significant pressures are in services supporting vulnerable children, particularly residential placements for children in care and home to school transport. Together, these areas are projecting an overspend of nearly £10m.

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Planned revenue savings for 2026-27 are tracking at 84% delivery, leaving a £5.6m variance from the £44.5m plan, with black-rated savings totalling £1.2m not achieving at all.
findings.detail: The council planned £44.5m in savings across the year but is now forecasting only £38.9m will be delivered. The shortfall is distributed across red, amber and black ratings. Major areas of under-delivery include children's placements (£0.6m delay in accommodation provision), home to school transport logistics (£1.6m), and adults services in-house review (£0.9m). While some shortfalls are being mitigated by underspends elsewhere, this creates risk to the council's ability to manage further in-year pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether planned efficiency and demand management actions are landing as forecast, as savings shortfalls are typically a precursor to further overspends.
findings.figures: £38.9m forecast savings against £44.5m plan (84%), £5.6m variance, black savings £1.2m
findings.quote: Currently, the council is forecasting to deliver £38.9m of savings against its original plan of £44.5m (84%). Savings that are off track have commentaries in the detailed savings tracker.

findings.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £159.8m cumulatively, generating £6.3m annual financing costs, and the government's grant submission was rejected in September.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit opened at £96.5m and is forecast to increase by £63.3m in-year, creating a £159.8m cumulative position. This is ringfenced and does not affect the general fund balance, but it forces external borrowing faster than otherwise needed, costing £6.3m in debt financing annually. Government promised to fund up to 90% of historical deficits conditional on a recovery plan, but Cambridgeshire's June submission was rejected; resubmission is planned for October 2026 with no confirmation of timing for any grant receipt.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on whether external deficits driven by demand that the council cannot control will erode cash and increase borrowing requirement, and whether government support will materialise.
findings.figures: £96.5m opening deficit, £63.3m in-year overspend, £159.8m closing deficit, £6.3m annual financing cost, submission rejected in June 2026
findings.quote: The 2026-27 DSG deficit is estimated to cost the Council £6.3m in debt financing costs, resulting from the reduction in actual cash available to the Council due to the deficit reducing the extent to which the Council can internally borrow from its working capital balances.

findings.quote: The general reserve, from which any overspend would be financed, is at its minimum acceptable level, and any utilisation of it would require top-up through next year's business planning process.

findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £63.3 million in-year deficit on the DSG, bringing the cumulative deficit to £96.5 million. The council applied to government for grant funding to cover up to 90% of the deficit through the end of 2025-26 but was not successful; government has requested further information.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit requiring annual borrowing or reserve funding; the failed grant application means the council cannot rely on government support to ease this burden
findings.figures: £63.3 million in-year deficit, £96.5 million cumulative, £6.3 million annual borrowing cost
findings.quote: The Council has not been successful in its initial application to government for grant funding to meet up to 90% of the deficit up to the end of 2025-26, with further information requested by government.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty preventing commissioning of independent risk management review.
findings.detail: The council declined to commission an independent external review of risk management, noting that LGR uncertainty creates a risk that review findings 'could become outdated or require significant revision as future governance arrangements are developed'. The council's external auditors KPMG have commented positively on risk management improvements.
findings.matters: LGR uncertainty affects the governance and financial arrangements of the organization; anyone lending to or partnering with the council needs visibility of this forward-looking structural risk.
findings.figures: Decision made September 2026; review decision to be kept under review
findings.quote: with the uncertainty regarding Local Government Reorganisation, there was a risk that findings or actions arising from such a review could become outdated or require significant revision as future governance arrangements are developed.

findings.headline: Service continuity risk from major incidents held at 20 following escalation from 12 in January.
findings.detail: Risk 4 (serious incident preventing services from operating or requiring major/critical incident response) increased from 12 in January to 20 by June, then remained static. The risk encompasses both operational incidents and climate-related events with potential for major service disruption.
findings.matters: Major incidents that prevent service operation create unplanned recovery costs and revenue loss, both of which affect financial outturn and cash position.
findings.figures: Risk score: 12 (January 2026), 20 (June onwards); static since June 2026
findings.quote: Risk that a serious incident occurs, preventing services from operating and /or requiring a major/critical incident response.

findings.headline: SEND statutory funding and DfE Safety Valve Agreement financial risk held at score 20, at maximum tolerable risk appetite.
findings.detail: Risk 15 (non-delivery of SEND statutory timelines, financial risk of the DfE Safety Valve Agreement for Cambridgeshire and increase in DSG spend) remains static at 20—the maximum level the council will tolerate. This represents an ongoing material financial exposure tied to statutory education commitments.
findings.matters: Safety Valve Agreements commit councils to defined spending on SEND; non-compliance triggers penalties or restrictions. DSG deficits are a nationwide pressure directly impacting council financial position.
findings.figures: Risk score: 20 (static since January 2026)
findings.quote: Non-delivery of SEND statutory timelines, financial risk of the DfE Safety Valve Agreement for Cambridgeshire and increase in DSG spend.

findings.headline: Budget sufficiency risk increased to 16 due to uncertainty on High Needs Stability Grant funding for 2026-28.
findings.detail: Risk 3 escalated from 12 to 16. The council has reserves to cover forecast deficits to March 2026, but faces 'a lack of clarity on the position for the current and future year with no provision'. The council believes 100% of High Needs funding should be provided by Central Government.
findings.matters: Budget adequacy is fundamental to financial resilience; a council unable to afford its planned objectives faces either spending cuts or further reserve depletion, affecting creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Risk score: 12 (June 2026) to 16 (September 2026); deficit period extends to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: At this stage the Council has reserves to cover what it forecasts to be the position up to 31 March 2026, however there is still a lack of clarity on the position for the current and future year with no provision.

findings.headline: KPMG external audit found overall improvement and no identified recommendations
findings.detail: In reviewing external audit findings as part of developing the updated risk management strategy, KPMG's assessment found overall improvement in the council's position and identified no recommendations for remediation.
findings.matters: A clean external audit with no outstanding recommendations indicates effective financial and governance controls, which affects credit profile assessment and is relevant to peers monitoring audit outcomes.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Relevant external audit findings by KPMG were also reviewed, noting overall improvement and no identified recommendations

findings.headline: Cambridgeshire County Council will be absorbed into unitary councils on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: The Risk Management Strategy is scoped to 2026–2028 rather than the traditional three-year period because the council will be subject to Local Government Reorganisation. From 1 April 2028, new unitary councils will absorb Cambridgeshire County Council's functions, and the county council will cease to exist as a separate entity.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand how existing borrowing arrangements and obligations will be treated under the new structure and what entities will be their counterparties post-reorganization. Finance directors at other councils want to understand how peers are managing transitions of this scale.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: given the expectation that Cambridgeshire County Council will be subject to Local Government Reorganisation and new unitary Councils will absorb Cambridgeshire County Council's functions from 1st April 2028

findings.headline: 2025/26 outturn came in to £0.5m overspend, improved from forecast; P5 2026/27 overspend smaller than previous years
findings.detail: The 2025/26 final outturn was £0.5m overspend, better than the forecast position, reducing the need to draw from reserves and supporting financial sustainability. Period 5 2026/27 is showing a small overall overspend that is smaller than overspends recorded at the same point in previous years, and the council believes it can be managed through reserves if needed with minimal impact to sustainability. This suggests budget controls are tightening.
findings.matters: Direction of travel in budget control is as important to lenders as the current position. Improvement suggests governance is effective despite structural pressures.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £0.5m overspend (improved from forecast); P5 2026/27: small overspend, smaller than previous years at same stage
findings.quote: Outturn compiled and near to balanced for 2025/26 thus reduced the risk of need to draw from reserves relating to revenue. Capital also underspent. Budget Monitoring for P5 identifies a small overspend, smaller than previous years, and action is underway to address and can be managed through reserves at worst case with minimal impact to financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport and children's social care placements showing material forecast overspend at P5 2026/27, with additional actions required
findings.detail: The council is forecasting material overspends in Home to School Transport and children's social care placements budgets at Period 5 2026/27. These are market-driven pressures (rising prices for Children in Care noted as a national issue). A working group and action plan are being developed to address the forecast overspends.
findings.matters: Children's services are a major budget pressure for councils and volatile market costs can exhaust contingency. Material overspends this early in the year suggest controls may not be sufficient without intervention.
findings.figures: P5 2026/27 showing material forecast overspend; national market cost issue
findings.quote: Home to School Transport and children's social care placements markets continue to be challenged with a material forecast overspend reported at P5 2026/27 - additional actions required to address and working group looking at.

findings.headline: DSG deficit: Government has committed to funding c90% to 31 March 2026, but 2026/27 and 2027/28 funding remains uncertain; council holds £7.5m in reserves
findings.detail: The Safety Valve programme has ended. The Government released information suggesting it will fund c90% of the council's historic High Needs deficit, but this only addresses the backlog up to 31 March 2026. Later years 2026/27 and 2027/28 remain uncertain despite rising deficits. The council currently holds £7.5m in reserves as a buffer. Further Government confirmation is expected in October 2026.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a material liability on council balance sheets; the funding gap and its solution are critical to borrowing capacity and financial sustainability. Uncertainty about future years keeps this a high risk despite the near-term funding announcement.
findings.figures: c90% of deficit funded; only to 31/3/2026; £7.5m held in reserves; deficit continues to rise
findings.quote: The DSG override has now been confirmed as continuing to 31/3/2028 and the Government have released information suggestion c90% of the deficit will be funded. Further information is imminent and a verbal update may be necessary at October SR&P, it is hoped that this will significantly reduces the risk. However, at this stage this only addresses backlog up to 31 March 2026, later years 2026/27 and 2027/28 remain uncertain and with rising deficits this will remain a high issue for CCC.

findings.headline: 2025-26 outturn delivered within 0.1% of budget; £38.9m 2026-27 savings on track despite emerging pressures
findings.detail: The council delivered its 2025-26 revenue outturn within 0.1% of planned budget, the third consecutive year within 1%. Current-year savings and income plans for 2026-27 remain on track for delivery despite the emerging medium-term pressures outlined.
findings.matters: Demonstrates execution capability in a pressured environment; relevant to credibility of delivering £36m savings programme ahead
findings.figures: 0.1% variance in 2025-26 outturn; third consecutive year within 1%; £38.9m 2026-27 savings on track
findings.quote: Maintaining robust and proactive financial management, demonstrated by a 2025/26 revenue outturn within 0.1% of the planned budget, the third consecutive year within 1%, alongside a strengthened balance sheet. Savings and income plans of £38.9 million remain on track for delivery in 2026-27

findings.headline: General fund reserves projected to fall to £6.0m by end of 2029-30; LGR reserve of £5m noted as insufficient
findings.detail: Current projections show general fund reserves declining across the medium-term to £6.0m by 2029-30 under planned drawdowns. The council holds a £5m reserve for potential Local Government Reorganisation costs but acknowledges this would be insufficient should that programme continue; uncertainty has pushed back assumption on timing.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits absorption capacity for emerging risks or one-off costs; LGR uncertainty prevents full reserve planning
findings.figures: General fund reserves projected at £6.0m by 2029-30; LGR reserve approximately £5m
findings.quote: A reserve remains in place for Local Government Reorganisation, currently around £5m. This is not expected to be sufficient should that work need to continue, but at this stage the assumptions about when that spend may take place have been pushed back.

findings.headline: Extended producer responsibility waste funding now budgeted as continuing income on reducing trajectory
findings.detail: This income source commenced in 2025-26 and was initially budgeted as temporary pending clarity on longer-term arrangements. The council now has sufficient certainty to budget it as continuing, securing £4.6m in 2027-28 onwards, though at a gradually reducing level as packaging disincentives take effect.
findings.matters: Unexpected medium-term income stream helps close a material portion of the budget gap; declining trajectory affects future planning
findings.figures: £4.6m saving from continuation in 2027-28; reducing basis thereafter
findings.quote: This funding stream commenced in 2025-26 but was budgeted for as a temporary funding source as the longer-term position of the funding, including any new burdens, was not known. There is now sufficient certainty to budget for an income amount on a reducing basis, reflecting the disincentive for waste packaging production that underpins this funding.

findings.headline: £30.4m savings gap identified for 2027-28: £36m total requirement but only £5.6m of solutions currently identified
findings.detail: The updated budget position requires £36m of total savings to balance the budget. The current medium-term financial plan contains only £5.6m of identified savings, leaving £30.4m that must be identified through the budget-setting process, which does not yet detail how this will be closed.
findings.matters: The extent of unidentified savings signals the scale of service change or income-generation work required; indicates timing pressure
findings.figures: £36m savings requirement; £5.6m identified; £30.4m gap
findings.quote: £36m savings requirement, of which £5.6m is already identified within the medium-term plan leaving a gap of £30.4m

findings.headline: Children in care cost pressures rising despite flat caseloads, driven by shift towards higher-needs placements
findings.detail: While the overall number of children in care has not increased materially, the composition is shifting towards children with higher levels of need, requiring more expensive placement types. This structural change is reflected as a £4.1m separate rebaselining pressure for 2027-28.
findings.matters: Cost inflation from demand composition rather than volume is harder to manage through throughput efficiency; suggests constrained supply of appropriate placements
findings.figures: £4.1m children's services rebaselining pressure for 2027-28
findings.quote: In particular, the shift towards children in care having higher needs is increasing costs despite the overall number of people supported being fairly stable.

findings.headline: Council forecast to fund 10% share of accumulated dedicated schools grant deficit over £96m
findings.detail: The DSG deficit, which has accumulated to over £96m, is being funded partly from reserves with the council now budgeting for 10% of the total. A £6.0m provision for 2027-28 reflects this crystallising liability, and further annual deficits are expected to accumulate without national reforms.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are balance-sheet liabilities that constrain flexibility and reduce reserves; signals whether system reform may eventually shift these costs
findings.figures: Aggregate deficit over £96m; £6.0m provision in 2027-28
findings.quote: The council is expected to need to fund 10% of its aggregated dedicated schools grant up to the end of 2025-26. The deficit stood at over £96m, with part of the cost of funding the council's share of this already provided for in reserves. The council expects to need to fund at least 10% of deficits going forward that will continue to accumulate without national reforms.

findings.headline: £3.96m revenue overspend forecast for 2026-27 driven by children in care placement costs
findings.detail: Despite the overall number of children in care remaining stable, rising placement costs are creating significant pressure. Additional pressures from home to school transport and older people services are only partly offset by underspends elsewhere, affecting the baseline for 2027-28.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends crystallise into structural baseline pressures; indicates demand composition rather than volume is driving cost inflation
findings.figures: £3.96 million forecast revenue overspend at end of period five 2026-27
findings.quote: At the end of period five for 2026-27, the council is forecasting a revenue overspend of £3.96 million. The detailed causes of this are set out in the IFMR, but they predominantly relate to services within Children, Education and Families... more children have higher levels of needs and therefore require higher cost placements.

findings.headline: Budget gap for 2027-28 forecast at £30.4m, compared to £15.7m projected in February 2026
findings.detail: Updated projections for demand, inflation, children's services pressures and DSG deficit provision have increased the forecast budget gap significantly. The three-year medium-term gap has grown to approximately £125m from the February 2026 projections.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand the scale of savings required and pace of emerging pressures; signals how quickly fiscal gaps can open
findings.figures: £30.4m for 2027-28 (compared to £15.7m); approximately £125m over the medium-term
findings.quote: These updated projections give a much-increased budget gap for 2027-28 of over £30 million, and around £125 million over the medium-term, compared to the projections presented in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Elective home education numbers rising to 2,510 children, up 240 year-on-year, with pending Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill proposing to materially increase local authority oversight obligations
findings.detail: Post-pandemic trend continues with elective home education numbers rising from 2,270 to 2,510 (up 10.6%). The Children's Wellbeing and Schools Bill, progressing through Parliament with amendments backed in January 2026, proposes mandatory national registers, local authority consent requirements before child withdrawal from school, and enhanced inspection and safeguarding powers. The council states that if enacted, these reforms would significantly reshape responsibilities and increase administrative and case management requirements.
findings.matters: Pending legislation could materially expand local authority obligations and create unfunded or unbudgeted staffing requirements; rising EHE numbers combined with future policy tightening could require significant resource increases for compliance.
findings.figures: 2,510 children in elective home education (up from 2,270, increase of 10.6%)
findings.quote: If enacted, these changes would significantly reshape local authority responsibilities, strengthen safeguarding expectations, and increase administrative and case management requirements across EHE and wider Education Inclusion functions.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Customer complaints overdue at 19% baseline rate in first quarterly reporting period under new measurement arrangements
findings.detail: During Q1, 563 complaints were received with 107 (19%) not answered within target response timeframes. The paper attributes this to operational challenges in managing complaint investigations and coordinating responses across service areas. The council has implemented new governance measures including a rota system for complaint responders and dedicated SEND resource to improve timeliness. This is the first data point under new reporting arrangements establishing baseline performance.
findings.matters: Complaint timeliness is an indicator of operational capacity and governance effectiveness; a 19% overdue rate in a new baseline may signal service capacity constraints or coordination issues that could escalate into governance or reputational risk.
findings.figures: 19% overdue (107 of 563 complaints), 22% statutory, 59% non-statutory, 20% ombudsman cases
findings.quote: During Quarter 1, 563 complaints were received, of which 107 were not responded to within the expected response timeframe, resulting in 19% of complaints being reported as overdue.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Two-year-old early education funded entitlement participation at 67.4%, below target of 75%, with Cambridgeshire falling to 5th ranked among 11 statistical neighbors from 10th position in 2021
findings.detail: Participation in the 15-hour funded entitlement for disadvantaged families has declined from 73.2% to 67.4%, moving further from the 75% target. Cambridgeshire's comparative ranking has deteriorated significantly: the authority ranked 10th of 11 statistical neighbors in 2021 but now ranks 5th (i.e., mid-pack). The paper attributes decline to the 30-hour working parent entitlement cannibalizing demand and earnings thresholds failing to keep pace with minimum wage rises.
findings.matters: Relative ranking decline against statistical neighbors signals either service positioning issue or adverse policy environment response; funding for these services may be demand-based; declining participation in a support programme for disadvantaged families merits assessment of service viability.
findings.figures: 67.4% uptake (target 75%, down from 73.2%), Cambridgeshire ranked 5th of 11 statistical neighbors in 2025 vs 10th of 11 in 2021
findings.quote: When comparing our uptake to that of our statistical neighbours Cambridgeshire has gone from 10/11 in 2021 to 5/11 in 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Children in care demand forecast to remain above target in short and medium term despite current rate 0.1 below target of 51 per 10,000
findings.detail: Current rate of 50.9 per 10,000 is marginally below the target of 51, but is increasing (up from 50.4 previous quarter). The council explicitly forecasts that target achievement is unlikely in the short to medium term given demand pressures, despite the Families First Programme being proposed as potential mitigation. This signals expectations of sustained above-target volumes.
findings.matters: Looked-after children placements are significant budget items; sustained above-target volumes would require ongoing budget allocation; council's explicit forecast of unachievable targets suggests demand pressures may be structurally embedded.
findings.figures: 50.9 per 10,000 (target 51, up from 50.4), England mean 67.0, statistical neighbors mean 51.0
findings.quote: It is likely given the level of demand and comparative data that achieving the target of 51 children per 10,000 is unlikely to be met in the short to medium term.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Placement stability for children in care declined to 62% from 65.7%, with placement moves accelerating since February 2026
findings.detail: The percentage of children aged under 16 in care for more than 2.5 years who remain in the same placement for over 2 years fell from 65.7% to 62%, moving further from the 71% target. The council identifies a specific trend reversal: since February 2026, an increase in children experiencing one placement change within two years has been the primary driver of this decline. Placement moves carry cost implications and the shift represents a material deterioration.
findings.matters: Each placement change incurs costs; a trend toward more moves suggests either service capacity constraints in supporting stable placements or increasing case complexity; movement away from target is material to budget and service delivery planning.
findings.figures: 62.0% in current quarter, down from 65.7% previous quarter, target 71%, trend reversal visible from February 2026
findings.quote: Since February 2026, an increase in children experiencing one placement change within two years has been the main driver of the reduced percentage.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Appendix 1 - Q1 CYP committee performance report 2026-27
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan assessments completed within statutory timescale at 4.9%, down to lowest point despite rising output volumes
findings.detail: The service completed 70 EHCPs in June compared with 52 in April, indicating increasing throughput, but is completing assessments far below its 20% target for timeliness. This reflects a deliberate strategy to prioritize children waiting longest: 60 of the 70 assessments completed were more than 30 weeks overdue. The council notes that achievement of the target will require both clearing the backlog and increasing in-time completions as capacity expands.
findings.matters: Education, Health and Care plans are statutory services with significant cost and compliance implications; a persistent backlog indicates either unbudgeted demand or a capacity shortfall that may require service investment or resource reallocation.
findings.figures: 4.9% within 20-week target (target 20%), 70 EHCPs finalised in June vs 52 in April, 60 of 70 June assessments were 30+ weeks overdue
findings.quote: Of the 70 plans completed in June, 60 related to assessments that were more than 30 weeks overdue, while only 4 were completed within 20 weeks.

findings.headline: Five of ten indicators are performing at or better than target (Green status), including child protection plan rates below national average and in-house foster carer placements exceeding target.
findings.detail: Of the 10 indicators updated this quarter, 5 are rated Green. Key successes include: child protection plan numbers (22.9 per 10,000) are lower than statistical neighbours and national average; in-house foster carer placement rates exceed target; and first choice school placements improved for both primary and secondary pupils. These represent services meeting or exceeding targets in important areas.
findings.matters: A finance director needs a balanced picture of where services are delivering effectively as well as where pressures exist; these positive indicators show capacity to deliver on strategy.
findings.figures: 5 of 10 indicators rated Green; child protection rate: 22.9 per 10,000
findings.quote: Of the 10 indicators updated this quarter, 5 are rated as Green.

findings.headline: Two school performance indicators are suspended pending completion of data system updates following Ofsted framework changes in late 2025.
findings.detail: Indicators tracking the percentage of schools judged Good or Outstanding (primary and secondary) have not been updated this quarter. The Ofsted inspection framework was updated in late 2025 and datasets only recently released. Local reporting tools that process and generate KPI information are being updated to handle the format and content changes. Work is expected to be completed for next quarter's report.
findings.matters: A one-quarter reporting gap on school performance removes visibility on a key education outcome for finance directors monitoring council performance and signals that data systems are struggling to keep pace with external framework changes.
findings.figures: 2 indicators suspended; updates expected Q2 2026/27
findings.quote: The Ofsted school inspection framework was updated in late 2025 and the related datasets have only recently been released. Due to the scale of the changes to format and content updates are being made to the local reporting tools that process the data and generate the KPI information.

findings.headline: A new baseline complaint handling metric shows 19% of complaints (107 of 563 received in Q1) were not responded to within expected timeframes.
findings.detail: A newly introduced Strategic Key Performance Indicator for complaint response timeliness found 19% of complaints overdue in Q1. Of these, 22% were statutory complaints, 59% non-statutory, and 20% from Ombudsman investigations. The service attributes delays to demand volume, case complexity, and resource availability. SEND services and non-Education complaints have introduced dedicated resource and rota systems to improve performance. Q1 is establishing a baseline for future trend analysis.
findings.matters: Complaint handling performance is a governance and risk indicator; sustained high rates of overdue responses signal systemic capacity or process issues and risk external regulatory scrutiny.
findings.figures: Q1: 563 complaints received; 107 overdue (19%); of overdue: 22% statutory, 59% non-statutory, 20% Ombudsman
findings.quote: During Quarter 1, 563 complaints were received, of which 107 were not responded to within the expected response timeframe, resulting in 19% of complaints being reported as overdue.

findings.headline: Six of ten updated performance indicators declined this quarter, against four that improved, including attendance, NEET figures, and children in care numbers.
findings.detail: Indicators showing declining performance include: children in care numbers (up), placement stability, child protection re-referrals, EHCP assessments, young people NEET or Unknown, and pupil attendance across all school types. This represents a pattern of declining performance across multiple service areas, signalling underlying service pressures or capacity constraints.
findings.matters: A pattern of declining performance across multiple indicators suggests underlying service pressures or capacity constraints that have financial and operational implications.
findings.figures: 6 indicators declined, 4 improved, out of 10 updated this quarter
findings.quote: Of the 10 indicators updated this quarter, 6 indicators saw a decline in performance compared to their previous reporting period

findings.headline: Long-term placement stability for Children Looked After has declined, with increased single placement changes since February 2026 identified as the main driver.
findings.detail: The proportion of placements lasting longer than 2 years has decreased. The paper attributes this to cohort changes (children leaving care, reaching age thresholds) but notes that since February 2026, an increase in children experiencing one placement change within two years has been the principal factor reducing the percentage. The service has completed an audit to identify improvements needed.
findings.matters: Multiple placement moves increase costs per child and signal service capacity pressures; they also present safeguarding and outcomes risks.
findings.figures: Trend declining since February 2026; specific percentage not disclosed in main text
findings.quote: Since February 2026, an increase in children experiencing one placement change within two years has been the main driver of the reduced percentage.

findings.headline: EHCP assessment completion within statutory 20-week timeframe dropped to 4.9% in June, with only 4 of 70 plans completed on time.
findings.detail: The council is prioritising clearing a backlog of cases delayed beyond statutory timescales, resulting in only 4.9% of assessments completed within the 20-week statutory requirement in June. Of 70 plans finalised in June, 60 related to assessments more than 30 weeks overdue. The service reports this is a deliberate twin-track strategy to both reduce historic delays and maintain throughput, despite the impact on the headline performance metric.
findings.matters: Assessment delays beyond statutory timescales create legal and reputational risk, and the backlog represents significant ongoing service capacity demand that affects financial planning.
findings.figures: June performance: 4.9%; June completions: 70 plans (60 overdue by 30+ weeks, 4 within 20 weeks)
findings.quote: In June, 70 EHCPs were finalised, compared with 60 in May and 52 in April. Of the 70 plans completed in June, 60 related to assessments that were more than 30 weeks overdue, while only 4 were completed within 20 weeks.

findings.headline: Childcare Act 2006 Section 7 places absolute statutory duty on councils to secure free early years provision for eligible children
findings.detail: Section 7 of the Childcare Act 2006 places a 'hard-edged' absolute legal duty on local authorities to secure free early years provision. The paper states that 'Resource scarcity or lack of local childcare staff is legally not a valid defence for failing to deliver an absolute statutory duty.' Failure to provide required provision can result in judicial review, complaint to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman with potential financial remedies, or formal DfE investigation. This makes early years spending non-discretionary.
findings.matters: The council cannot reduce or defer this spending for budget reasons; legal duty creates a binding, non-negotiable budget commitment that cannot be escaped for financial constraints.
findings.figures: Childcare Act 2006 Section 7 (absolute duty) and Section 6 (sufficient childcare); Children and Families Act 2014 Section 42 (duty for children with EHCP)
findings.quote: Under Section 7 of the Childcare Act 2006, LAs have a 'hard-edged' absolute legal duty to secure free early years provision for eligible children

findings.headline: Most contracts run 5–10 years, extending to 2036–2037 beyond the planned April 2028 local government reorganisation.
findings.detail: The majority of contracts offer five-year initial terms with five-year extension options, running well into the post-reorganisation period. The paper acknowledges that 'the proposed term of these contracts extend beyond April 2028, beyond the timetable for Local Government Re-organisation as currently envisaged.' Officers justify longer terms as necessary to 'secure best value for money both now and in the future and support the resilience of the market,' with successor councils able to take over the contracts.
findings.matters: Long-term service commitments extending into the post-reorganisation period create both potential benefits (market stability) and execution risks (dependence on successor councils' willingness to novate), affecting continuity during local government structural change.
findings.figures: April 2028 planned reorganisation date; contracts extend to 2031–2037
findings.quote: It is recognised that the proposed term of these contracts extend beyond April 2028, beyond the timetable for Local Government Re-organisation as currently envisaged.

findings.headline: Contract revenues depend on capacity take-up; early years funded by demand-led DSG, wraparound entirely by parent opt-in.
findings.detail: The £28.8m contract values represent estimated provider income 'if operating at capacity within each setting.' Early years provision is funded from 'the early years block of the Dedicated Schools Grant which is based on actual take-up,' while wraparound provision is entirely 'funded by parents/carers who can opt in/out of the service.' Actual council spending will be lower if take-up falls below capacity or parents do not opt in.
findings.matters: The council's actual spend on these contracts is not fixed but depends on parental demand and service take-up, creating budget variability that cannot be predicted at approval.
findings.figures: Total value £28,763,997 at estimated capacity; wraparound contract example: Brampton £929,465 (entirely parent-funded)
findings.quote: The estimated spend relating to early years places will be funded from the early years single funding formula, from the early years block of the Dedicated Schools Grant which is based on actual take-up. Wraparound provision will be funded by parents/carers who can opt in/out of the service.

findings.headline: Three additional early years contracts worth £12.7m added since January 2026 due to building transfers, closures, and expiring contracts.
findings.detail: Since January 2026, three new contracts have been added: an Earith primary school building gifted to the council following pre-school closure (£3.54m full term), a new Nest facility in Cambridge following provider closure (£5.28m), and Kester Way in St Neots where the existing contract is expiring (£3.83m). The paper notes that 'changes to circumstances mean that an additional three contracts are required.'
findings.matters: Shows the council's early years capacity and service needs are changing faster than the January planning cycle anticipated, requiring additional budget allocation mid-year.
findings.figures: £3,542,452 (Earith full term) + £5,282,400 (Nest full term) + £3,832,800 (Kester Way full term) = £12,657,652
findings.quote: changes to circumstances mean that an additional three contracts are required

findings.headline: Contract values repriced in March 2026 due to funding rate changes, requiring return to committee; new 10% delegation threshold approved.
findings.detail: The contract values in the current recommendation differ from those presented to committee in January 2026 because funding rates changed. To prevent future returns to committee for similar rate changes, the recommendation includes a new 10% delegation threshold allowing officers to adjust contract values within this range without committee approval.

findings.paper_title: Inclusion for All - Resetting the improvement programme to align with the DfE SEND Reform Plan and key local priorities
findings.headline: Pathfinder Legal Services unable to provide further SEND legal support; council must commission alternative legal advisers, creating financial and continuity risks.
findings.detail: Pathfinder Legal Services has advised it cannot provide further SEND legal support. The council has had to commission alternative external legal advisers, creating additional financial, capacity and continuity risks. SEND-related legal activity is placing pressure on the corporate legal budget, driven by increases in legal challenges requiring external advice and representation, and regulatory or court-related financial penalties. Loss of an established legal service provider in a growing area of litigation creates both unbudgeted procurement costs and operational risk.
findings.matters: Loss of an established legal service provider in a high-cost and growing area of legal exposure creates unplanned procurement costs and operational risk in managing SEND-related litigation.
findings.figures: SEND-related legal activity creating pressure on corporate legal budget; specific costs not separately disclosed
findings.quote: Pathfinder Legal Services has advised that it is not able to provide support for further SEND legal cases. The Council has therefore needed to commission alternative external legal advisers to provide advice and representation in relation to SEND matters. This position creates additional financial, capacity and continuity risks.

findings.paper_title: Inclusion for All - Resetting the improvement programme to align with the DfE SEND Reform Plan and key local priorities
findings.headline: Interim allocation of £4.837m released to mainstream schools affected by delayed EHCP assessments; permanent funding model still to be determined.
findings.detail: The council has released an initial £4.837m interim allocation to mainstream schools experiencing the greatest pressure from delayed EHCP assessments. Further work is required with school leaders to determine the next iteration of the funding model, including consideration of backdating and adjustment of proxy indicators. The one-off nature of this allocation creates ongoing budget uncertainty for both the council and schools.
findings.matters: The allocation addresses a symptom of the EHCP backlog but does not establish a sustainable funding settlement, leaving the council's budget exposed to continued pressure and schools uncertain of future support.
findings.figures: £4.837m interim allocation to mainstream schools
findings.quote: In parallel, an initial £4.837m targeted interim allocation has been released to support mainstream schools experiencing the greatest pressure from delayed EHCP assessments.

findings.paper_title: Inclusion for All - Resetting the improvement programme to align with the DfE SEND Reform Plan and key local priorities
findings.headline: Up to £2.0m recovery investment proposed for EHCP delayed assessments; 2,370 cases over 20-week timescale as at August 2026, forecast to increase to 3,340 within twelve months without intervention.
findings.detail: As at 17 August 2026, 2,370 of 3,102 live EHCP assessments were over the statutory 20-week timescale, including 321 exceeding 100 weeks. Without additional recovery capacity, the number over 20 weeks is forecast to increase to around 2,690 within six months and 3,340 within twelve months. The proposed recovery programme has a potential envelope of up to £2.0m over 12 months, with an initial £495k proof-of-concept phase. Progression beyond the proof-of-concept is conditional on evidence of effectiveness, affordability and scalability.
findings.matters: Substantial investment is required to address EHCP delays that drive legal risk, complaints, tribunal activity and cost pressures; recovery is critical to achieving the council's financial sustainability objectives.
findings.figures: Up to £2.0m over 12 months; £495k proof-of-concept gateway; 2,370 assessments over 20 weeks as at 17 August 2026, including 321 over 100 weeks
findings.quote: The proposed response is a single delayed-assessment recovery programme of up to £2.000m over 12 months, with a £495k 'proof-of-concept' investment operating as the first gateway.

findings.paper_title: Inclusion for All - Resetting the improvement programme to align with the DfE SEND Reform Plan and key local priorities
findings.headline: Independent and non-maintained special school placement costs increased 46 per cent to £33.7m for 531 pupils between November 2024 and July 2026.
findings.detail: Cambridgeshire's expenditure on independent and non-maintained special provision has escalated significantly. Between November 2024 and July 2026 (eight months), pupil numbers in this sector increased from 373 to 531 and associated costs rose from £23.0m to £33.7m, with average unit costs rising slightly from £61,764 to £63,515 per pupil. The council recognizes over-reliance on high-cost independent provision and is implementing a capital-led strategy to reduce dependence through expansion of maintained special schools and specialist resource bases.
findings.matters: Rapid escalation in this high-cost category represents the primary driver of the council's High Needs DSG deficit and the core financial sustainability challenge across the local SEND system.

findings.headline: Approval of Local SEND Reform Plan deferred pending revision by 30 November 2026; access to High Needs Stability Grant conditional on DfE approval.

findings.matters: Access to a grant intended to cover 90% of the accrued High Needs DSG deficit is now contingent on meeting a specific revision deadline, creating timing and compliance risk in a key funding stream for addressing an accumulated financial problem.

The timeline for submission of that additional information is 30 November 2026.

findings.headline: Council establishing single supplier contracts for executive search and senior interim workers in preparation for anticipated senior-level turnover due to Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty
findings.detail: The council is consolidating senior recruitment through pre-agreed single suppliers to enable faster recruitment and maintain service continuity in anticipation of potential increased turnover driven by Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty.
findings.matters: Anticipated senior-level turnover risk is material to lenders and peer councils, as it could drive higher agency costs and service continuity challenges across the authority.
findings.figures: Executive search spend past 3 years: £233k. Senior interim spend outside framework past 12 months: £419,706.
findings.quote: With ongoing uncertainty due to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), it is possible that the Council's turnover will start to increase and this could be at a senior level.

findings.detail: The council must finance any overspend from general reserves that are constrained by a legal minimum set under s25 of the Local Government Act 2003. Use of reserves for the current overspend impacts the Chief Financial Officer's assessment of reserve adequacy in subsequent years.

findings.matters: A large static DSG variance reflects system-wide underfunding of schools that the council cannot resolve; other councils and lenders need to understand that this is a persistent pressure on the authority's overall sustainability.

findings.detail: The principal risk—managing SEND statutory duties and DSG financial exposure—remains scored at 20 (High Impact 4, Very Likely 5), unchanged over six months. findings.quote: Key expenditure controls are in place.
