findings.headline: LED lantern replacement project delivering £1,785k street lighting energy savings against planned target of £301k; savings over-delivered by £1,484k.
findings.detail: Year-to-date electricity usage is approximately half that of the same period in the prior year. Savings further boosted by annual electricity charge adjustment (May 2026), PFI contract pension reconciliation (July 2026), and LED-related maintenance efficiencies. Additional smaller reductions anticipated as LED rollout continues.
findings.matters: Early and material over-delivery on a major capital investment confirms energy efficiency benefits are exceeding expectations and validates the investment case.
findings.figures: Planned £301k, forecast £1,785k (£1,484k over-delivery, 493% variance)
findings.quote: Savings reflect reduced energy consumption from the ongoing LED lantern replacement project. Year to date usage is approximately half that of the same period in the prior year. Further smaller reductions may be realised as the LED rollout continues.

findings.headline: Road network condition deteriorating on majority of road types, with A, C and U roads worsening from previous assessment
findings.detail: A roads reached 22% in amber/red condition against 20% target (declining); C roads at 34.6% versus 33.8% target (declining); U roads at 36.3% versus 35% target (declining); only B roads improved slightly to 34% from 35%. Council has switched from GAIST to SCANNER survey methodology, which uses more detailed laser/sensor measurements and is not directly comparable to recent data, but permits better long-term trend analysis.
findings.matters: Worsening asset condition across most road types suggests deferred maintenance; the council notes that treating roads in amber condition is 'much more cost effective than letting a location reach RED', implying escalating future maintenance costs if this trend continues.
findings.figures: A roads 22.1% (target 20%); B roads 34% (target 35%); C roads 34.6% (target 33.8%); U roads 36.3% (target 35%)
findings.quote: Generally the aim is to keep as much of the network in the Amber / Green category by directing funding / resources to treating the Ambers as this is much more cost effective than letting a location reach RED which then requires more expensive and extensive repairs.

findings.headline: Public satisfaction with highways services declining or flat across all measures despite £43m additional investment over two years
findings.detail: Overall satisfaction held at 45% (meeting newly raised target), but component measures weakened: road safety satisfaction at 48% (down from 55% in 2021-22); highways maintenance satisfaction at 42% (down from 46%); active travel satisfaction flat at 50%. Declining satisfaction despite stated investment suggests underlying service issues persist.
findings.matters: Deteriorating public perception of core services indicates either that investment is not addressing resident concerns or that service quality pressures are outpacing funding; continued decline could drive political pressure for further resource allocation.
findings.figures: Overall 45% (target 45%, previous 36%); Road Safety 48% (previous 54%); Highways Maintenance 42% (previous 46%); Active Travel 50%; £43m additional investment committed over two years
findings.quote: We have allocated an additional £43m towards highway maintenance over the last two years.

findings.headline: Killed or seriously injured road casualties increased to 370 annually versus 272 target, with council unable to track toward 2030 Vision Zero goal
findings.detail: The 12-month rolling total is now 370 casualties (target 272, previous 322), representing deteriorating performance. The council's commentary explicitly states the trend is unlikely to achieve the 50% reduction target set by the Vision Zero Partnership for 2030 if it continues.
findings.matters: A major policy failure against an agreed partnership target; indicates the council's road safety strategy is not delivering and may require significant intervention or investment to reverse course.
findings.figures: 370 current (12-month rolling total) vs 272 target vs 322 previous comparable period
findings.quote: At the time of reporting, the overall trend for KSIs is not improving. If the trend continues then it is unlikely we will achieve the 50% reduction target set by the Vision Zero Partnership for 2030.

findings.headline: Highways maintenance defects repair rate at 63% against 90% target, with 8,664 potholes awaiting repair
findings.detail: Performance fell from 89% in October 2025 to 28% in January 2026 before recovering to 68% by May; a further drop to 63% in June indicates renewed pressure. The council has committed to clearing the full backlog by end of October 2026, creating an imminent deadline that flags resource pressure for the coming months.
findings.matters: A service rated 27 percentage points below target (triggering a red rating) indicates significant asset maintenance stress; the tight October deadline suggests the council will need to concentrate resources to deliver on this commitment, with potential knock-on effects on other capital work.
findings.figures: 63% current performance vs 90% target (previous 68%); 8,664 potholes awaiting repair; 6,848 repaired in June
findings.quote: As of the end of June, the number of potholes awaiting repair stands at 8,664. During June, 6,848 potholes were repaired.

findings.headline: Safer Routes to Schools scheme deliberately paused for stakeholder engagement, rephasing £580k capital spend
findings.detail: A larger Safer Routes to Schools scheme within the Safety Schemes programme has been paused to facilitate further engagement with local Members and stakeholders. This generates a £580k underspend on Highways & Transport capital schemes, with expenditure rephased into future years, remaining within the capital variations budget.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders distinguish between capital slippage due to delivery problems and deliberate programme pauses for engagement; this shows Cambridgeshire managing its capital programme actively rather than slipping, and maintaining flexibility to incorporate stakeholder feedback.
findings.figures: £580k underspend
findings.quote: This reflects the pausing of a larger Safer Routes to Schools scheme to facilitate further engagement with local Members and stakeholders, resulting in expenditure being rephased into future years.

findings.headline: Street Lighting forecast underspend of £1.97m driven by LED replacement programme efficiency gains
findings.detail: The LED lantern replacement programme is delivering reduced electricity consumption within the Street Lighting budget. Additional savings have arisen through annual electricity charge adjustment recalculation, PFI pension reconciliation, and reduced maintenance costs associated with the LED rollout.
findings.matters: Finance directors at peer councils managing similar street lighting services would want to understand how LED programmes can deliver measurable efficiency savings, and lenders see this as evidence of the council's ability to execute capital programmes that generate ongoing operational savings.
findings.figures: £1.97m underspend
findings.quote: The most significant issue is the forecast underspend on Street Lighting of £1.97m, driven primarily by reduced electricity consumption resulting from the ongoing LED lantern replacement programme. Additional savings have arisen through the annual electricity charge adjustment recalculation, PFI pension reconciliation and reduced maintenance costs associated with the LED rollout.

findings.headline: Killed or seriously injured casualties indicator red, 10% or more from target
findings.detail: The 12-month rolling total of KSI road casualties is not meeting the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Road Safety Strategy target. The council is working with the Vision Zero Partnership, Cambridgeshire Constabulary and the Combined Authority to address this through targeted interventions including young driver and older driver workshops, motorcycle safety courses, and bikeability training. The council intends to review the role of the Vision Zero Partnership to enhance its effectiveness.
findings.matters: Road safety targets are statutory obligations; failure to meet them carries legal consequences and indicates service delivery pressure affecting public safety and the council's legal liability.
findings.figures: H&T 004 status: Red (10%+ from target)
findings.quote: In order to achieve the targets set out in the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Road Safety Strategy, a partnership approach is required with active contribution from those in the Vision Zero Partnership (VZP), most notably the Cambridgeshire Constabulary and the CPCA together with the Council as the Highways Authority.

findings.headline: New AI governance risks added July 2026 for both officers and members.
findings.detail: Two new AMBER risks (3,3) added July 2026: Risk 20a 'Inappropriate use of AI by officers or external service providers in fund management, administration, and governance activities' and Risk 7d 'Inappropriate use of AI by scheme members'. Risks include data breaches, AI hallucinations, member susceptibility to scams, and reputational damage. Mitigations include staff training, website safeguards, and member warnings, mostly completed or in progress.
findings.matters: Emerging AI risks create new vectors for data loss, compliance failure, and member harm; technology governance gaps could trigger regulatory concern.
findings.figures: Risk 20a AMBER (3,3), added July 2026; Risk 7d AMBER (3,3), added July 2026
findings.quote: Inappropriate use of AI by officers or external service providers in fund management, administration, and governance activities.

findings.headline: Independent Person recruitment for Pensions Committee at AMBER risk against 31 October 2026 deadline for Fit for the Future compliance
findings.detail: Risk 16a 'The Fund may not be able to recruit an Independent Person as a non-voting member of the Pensions Committee in the required timescale' is AMBER (3,3). This is a regulatory requirement for Fit for the Future compliance. Mitigations include considering existing advisors, widening recruitment channels, and accelerating internal processes. Current status shows recruitment 'in progress' with note: 'working on appointment of Independent Person before deadline.'
findings.matters: Failure to appoint an Independent Person by 31 October 2026 would breach regulatory requirements for fund governance, creating compliance and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Risk 16a AMBER (3,3); deadline 31 October 2026
findings.quote: The Fund may not be able to recruit an Independent Person as a non-voting member of the Pensions Committee in the required timescale

findings.headline: Regulatory and scheme changes compressed into tight timescale create implementation risk.
findings.detail: Risks 18a and 19a both AMBER (3,3) identify that the volume of regulatory changes and delayed LGPS guidance create capacity pressure to implement mandatory changes safely within deadlines. Risk 18a states: 'The volume of scheme changes being introduced through new regulations and guidance over a compressed timescale puts at risk the administering authority's ability to manage and administer the Fund in an effective manner'. Fund has escalated project resource and prioritisation, but risk remains material.
findings.matters: Implementation failures or delays in mandatory regulatory changes trigger compliance breaches with potential for Pensions Regulator enforcement action and member harm.
findings.figures: Risk 18a AMBER (3,3); Risk 19a AMBER (3,3); both relating to compressed implementation timescales in 2026
findings.quote: The volume of scheme changes being introduced through new regulations and guidance over a compressed timescale puts at risk the administering authority's ability to manage and administer the Fund in an effective manner

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation poses structural uncertainty to fund administration arrangements.
findings.detail: Risk 17a identifies that LGR may adversely impact fund management and administration due to 'additional workloads and constitutional changes, including the identification of a new administering authority'. Rated AMBER (4,2). Early information sharing is in progress, but broader integration with the LGR project plan and identification of a new administering authority remains future activity, creating transition risk for fund governance.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation could affect the fund's administration, governance arrangements, and service continuity; failure to plan the pension implications of LGR could disrupt contribution collection and benefit payments.
findings.figures: Risk 17a AMBER (Impact 4, Likelihood 2)
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation may adversely impact Fund management and administration due to additional workloads and constitutional changes, including the identification of a new administering authority

findings.headline: Loss of key manager and ongoing sickness absence driving staffing risk to AMBER.
findings.detail: Risk 3d 'Unable to deliver pension services due to inadequate recruitment/retention processes' remains at AMBER (3,3) despite multiple mitigations. The Fund explicitly notes: 'Current risk remains at 9 due to sickness management and losing a key Manager in the service.' Mitigations include recruitment via agencies, establishment increases, and succession planning, but cannot offset the loss of key personnel affecting operational capacity.
findings.matters: Staffing capacity directly affects pension administration service delivery, financial controls, and data quality, which are essential to fund soundness and member protection.
findings.figures: Risk 3d AMBER (3,3); current risk score 9; key manager loss ongoing
findings.quote: Current risk remains at 9 due to sickness management and losing a key Manager in the service.

findings.headline: Pensions Committee member training deadline missed in June 2026, heightening governance risk.
findings.detail: Risk 3a 'Those charged with governance are unable to fulfil their responsibilities effectively' was heightened to AMBER status in June 2026 after member training failed to complete by the required deadline. The Fund notes: 'June 2026 - Risk heightened due member training not being completed by the deadline.' The Fund is addressing this through enhanced training strategies and knowledge assessments, but the missed deadline signals a temporary control gap affecting governance capacity.
findings.matters: Governance training quality directly affects the Pensions Committee's ability to make informed financial and investment decisions, and weak governance oversight creates compliance and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Risk 3a current rating AMBER (Impact 4, Likelihood 3); heightened June 2026
findings.quote: June 2026 - Risk heightened due member training not being completed by the deadline.

findings.headline: Employer contribution rates to the pension fund reduced at 2025 valuation due to surplus funding positions.
findings.detail: The 2025 actuarial valuation set lower primary and secondary contribution rates for employers, reflecting improved funding positions within the scheme. Despite this rate reduction, actual 2026/27 contributions are forecast £1.1m above budget (£151m vs £149.9m), likely due to salary growth and membership factors.
findings.matters: Lower employer contribution rates reduce the council's ongoing pension cost obligations, freeing budget capacity; improved fund solvency also strengthens the council's overall financial position and reduces future funding risk.
findings.figures: Contributions budget £149,900k; forecast £151,000k; contribution rates reduced at 2025 valuation
findings.quote: Contributions in 2026/27 are the new contribution rates set at 2025 valuation; primary and secondary contribution rates have reduced for employers due to surplus funding positions.

findings.headline: Investment management expenses £272k over budget: CBRE costs increased since January 2026 but not budgeted.
findings.detail: Total investment expenses forecast £1.553m against budget £1.281m (21% overspend). CBRE's service costs rose from January 2026 onwards but the cost increase was not reflected in the 2026/27 budget, indicating either forecasting weakness or emerging cost pressure.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted cost increases in a material expense category signal either control weaknesses or structural cost pressures; a lender would want to understand whether this is one-off or indicates higher ongoing management costs.
findings.figures: Total investment expenses budget £1,281k; forecast £1,553k; variance (£272k)
findings.quote: CBRE expenses have increased since January 2026; however, this increase was not reflected in the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast £71.3m, £22.7m (24%) below budget of £94m.
findings.detail: The shortfall is explained by exclusion of a large distribution received in 2025/26. The finance director must understand whether this underperformance will require increased council contributions to the fund. The forecast applies the standard actuarial assumption of 6% growth to 2025/26 forecasts.
findings.matters: A significant shortfall in pension fund investment returns may force the council to increase employer contributions, creating budget pressure that affects the council's cash position and debt service capacity.
findings.figures: Investment income budget £94,000k; forecast £71,293k; variance (£22,707k)
findings.quote: Investment income has been calculated based on the 2025/26 forecast by applying the actuarial assumption of investment growth +6% per annum. The Fund received a large distribution during 2025/26, which has been excluded from estimates for subsequent years as details are not yet confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 -Appendix 1
findings.headline: Successfully connected to Pensions Dashboard regulatory infrastructure ahead of statutory deadline
findings.detail: All LGPS funds were required to connect to the Pensions Dashboard infrastructure by 31 October 2025. The Cambridgeshire Fund 'successfully connected to the Pensions Dashboards infrastructure ahead of the statutory deadline' and continues undertaking post-connection activities. The Chair describes the Dashboards as 'one of the most significant developments affecting the pensions industry' requiring 'extensive preparation across the sector'.
findings.matters: Meeting regulatory deadlines ahead of schedule demonstrates effective governance and compliance management. This reduces regulatory risk and shows the Fund is managing complex national policy changes competently.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline 31 October 2025; Fund connected ahead of deadline; wider public access planned 2027-28
findings.quote: I am pleased to report that the Fund successfully connected to the Pensions Dashboards infrastructure ahead of the statutory deadline and continues to undertake post-connection activities in preparation for wider public access Dashboards during 2027-28.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 -Appendix 1
findings.headline: Exceptional contribution collection with 99.6% of employer and employee payments received on time
findings.detail: Of total contributions of £171.5m, 99.6% (£170.8m) was received on time, with only £688k (0.4%) paid late. The paper notes the Fund 'did not apply any additional charges or levies in respect of contributions received late, and no reports were made to The Pensions Regulator in respect of late contributions during the year'. This demonstrates strong employer compliance and effective fund administration.
findings.matters: Strong on-time contribution collection reduces cash management complexity and regulatory risk. Late contributions create liquidity issues and potential regulatory reporting obligations, so a 99.6% on-time rate shows excellent operational control and employer engagement.
findings.figures: Total contributions £171.5m; on-time £170.8m (99.6%); late £0.688m (0.4%); zero Pensions Regulator reports
findings.quote: Of the total amount of contributions received, only 0.4% (£688k) was paid late by employers.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 -Appendix 1
findings.headline: Fund achieved strong 6.6% investment return generating £378m gain despite market volatility
findings.detail: The Fund returned 6.6% on its investments during the year, generating £378.1m of investment gain. Additional investment income was £86.4m. This strong performance occurred during a period the Chair describes as containing 'ongoing economic uncertainty and market volatility'. The positive return demonstrates effective asset allocation and investment management, partly offsetting the funding ratio decline.
findings.matters: Strong investment returns reduce the need for increased employer contributions to meet funding targets and provide a buffer against future market downturns. This positive performance in difficult conditions demonstrates effective fund stewardship.
findings.figures: 6.6% investment return; £378.1m investment gain; £86.4m investment income; return on £5.26bn of assets
findings.quote: The Fund returned 6.6% on investments during the year resulting in a £378.1m return on investments.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 -Appendix 1
findings.headline: Forced migration to Border to Coast pooling following government rejection of ACCESS proposal created unbudgeted governance costs
findings.detail: Following the Government's 'Fit for the Future' reforms requiring all pools to be FCA-regulated investment management companies, ACCESS Pool submitted a proposal in April 2025 which was rejected. The Fund was forced to identify an alternative pool and completed transition to Border to Coast Pensions Partnership (BCPP) by the government deadline of 1 April 2026. The Chair describes this as 'momentous structural change' requiring 'considerable work'. Oversight and governance costs were £1,616k against a budget of £1,408k — a £208k overspend — with the paper specifically citing 'unplanned expenditure arising from the Government's Fit for the Future agenda following the rejection of ACCESS's proposal'.
findings.matters: A forced change to pooling arrangements creates operational risk and demonstrates limited control over cost outcomes when government mandates structural change. The unbudgeted £208k spend shows transition complexity. This represents a material governance change affecting investment implementation and cost structure going forward.
findings.figures: Oversight and governance costs £1,616k actual vs £1,408k budget (£208k overspend); transition completed 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Oversight and governance costs are higher than expected due to unplanned expenditure arising from the Government's Fit for the Future agenda following the rejection of ACCESS's proposal in April 2025.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026 -Appendix 1
findings.headline: Funding level fell from 147% to 132% in one year despite £355m asset growth and 6.6% investment returns
findings.detail: The Fund's formal actuarial valuation at 31 March 2025 reported a funding level of 147%. Monitoring undertaken one year later at 31 March 2026 showed the funding level had fallen to 132%, a decline of 15 percentage points, despite total assets increasing by £355.2m (to £5.26bn) and investment returns of 6.6% generating £378.1m. The paper attributes this only to 'movements in the Fund's assets and liabilities' but provides no explanation of the cause — whether from discount rate changes, actuarial assumption updates, or other factors. This suggests liabilities grew faster than assets despite positive investment performance.
findings.matters: A significant decline in funding ratio in a single year indicates something material has changed in the pension fund's position. If this trend continues, it could necessitate increased employer contribution rates to maintain adequate funding, directly affecting the council's budget.
findings.figures: Funding level 147% at 31 March 2025; 132% at 31 March 2026; asset growth £355.2m; investment return 6.6%; investment gain £378.1m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, updated funding monitoring undertaken between formal valuations indicated a funding level of 132%, reflecting movements in the Fund's assets and liabilities since the 2025 valuation.

findings.headline: Risk index has increased from 303 to 314, with two additional risks now on the register.
findings.detail: The council's aggregate risk position has deteriorated. The risk index rose 3.6% since the previous report, and the total number of risks increased from 41 to 43. The breakdown remains predominantly low and medium risks, with no high-risk items currently flagged.
findings.matters: A worsening risk profile signals that the council's operational or strategic environment is becoming more constrained or uncertain, which affects its operational resilience and ability to deliver.
findings.figures: Risk Index current 314, previous 303; total risks 43, previous 41; low-risk 22, medium-risk 21, high-risk 0
findings.quote: Current Risk Index  314 Previous Risk Index  303 Total risks   43 Previous number of risks 41

findings.headline: Pensions Regulator compliance assessment identified gaps in risk management and member information disclosure.
findings.detail: A General Code of Practice self-assessment conducted by the Pensions Service and verified by Hymans Robertson found compliance to be generally good but noted areas requiring improvement in risk management and information to members. The Head of Pensions committed to further reporting on remedial progress.
findings.matters: The Pensions Regulator's Code sets minimum governance standards for LGPS funds; identified gaps indicate regulatory risk and the need for corrective action.
findings.figures: Self-assessment completed in 2024; verified by Hymans Robertson; reported to Pension Fund Committee October 2024
findings.quote: Compliance was generally found to be good, with some areas for improvement in risk management and information to members.

findings.headline: Benefits Administration audit frequency is being reduced from annual to biennial review, despite it being the highest-transactional and fraud-risk area of the fund.
findings.detail: The Internal Audit team proposes reducing audits of Benefits Administration (new starters, transfers, deceased pensioners, payments) to every two years with a smaller work programme, based on prior audits achieving consistently good ratings. This represents a material change from historical practice.
findings.matters: Benefits Administration is the pension fund operation with the greatest exposure to fraud, error and controls failure; reducing audit frequency delays detection of control degradation or emerging issues.
findings.figures: Frequency change from annual to biennial; audit scope budgeted at 30 days for 2026/7
findings.quote: As considerable audit focus over the past several years has been given to benefits administration, and this area has consistently obtained a 'good' assurance rating, the intention is that audits of benefits administration will reduce in frequency to take place every 2 years, with a slightly reduced work programme.

findings.headline: External audit identified control weaknesses in the pension fund's IT system around user access rights and monitoring of high-risk activities.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's audit of the Altair system for Northamptonshire Pension Fund, conducted to support the financial statement audit, identified risks in user access controls and monitoring. Actions were agreed with management but their implementation status is not reported in this document.
findings.matters: IT system controls are foundational to preventing fraud and error in pension fund operations; weak access controls and activity monitoring increase risk of misappropriation or data integrity failures.
findings.figures: Audit covered year ended 31 March 2024
findings.quote: This audit identified some risks around user access rights and monitoring of high-risk activities, with actions agreed to address these risks.

findings.headline: Internal audit delivery fell short of plan in 2025/6 due to staffing shortage in the audit team, leaving reviews of cash, treasury and project management incomplete.
findings.detail: Only 42 audit days were delivered against a planned 53. The shortfall occurred because staffing constraints in the first half of 2025/6 prevented completion of Cash & Treasury Management and Project Management audits. These are scheduled to be completed in Q1 2026/7.
findings.matters: Planned oversight of key operational and financial risk areas did not occur as scheduled, creating a gap in assurance over fund controls during the period.
findings.figures: 42 days delivered vs. 53 planned; 20.8% shortfall
findings.quote: Overall, the audit time delivered to the Funds in 2025/6 has been lower than planned, with 42 days delivered rather than the 53 originally expected.

findings.headline: Three fraud control actions from the 2023/4 Benefits Administration audit have been implemented, closing gaps in pension payment controls.
findings.detail: The Pensions Service has completed implementation of controls to verify genuine official documents (birth/marriage certificates), deployed bank verification software for pension transfers and payments, and arranged mortality screening for overseas pensioners. All agreed actions from the 2023/4 audit are now complete.
findings.matters: Pension fund fraud directly threatens fund solvency and creates contingent liability for the employer; completion of recommended controls is a positive indicator of governance follow-through.
findings.figures: Three actions completed; all agreed audit actions from 2023/4 Benefits Administration review now implemented
findings.quote: The implementation of these three actions represents a strengthening of the control environment and a reduction in the risk of fraud for the Funds. It also means that all agreed audit actions from the review of Benefits Administration have now been implemented

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Monitoring Report Quarter to 30 June 2026 (Public Version)
findings.headline: UBS Infrastructure holding returned -14.9% per annum over three years against 8.2% benchmark target
findings.detail: The UBS Infrastructure holding has delivered negative returns of -14.9% per annum over three years while the benchmark was 8.2%, representing a 23 percentage point annualized shortfall. The mandate also returned -9.0% in Q2 2026 alone. This persistent underperformance across a £374m holding (7% of the fund) raises questions about asset quality and manager competence.
findings.matters: Large losses in alternative assets earmarked to deliver long-term value reduce the fund's return capacity and force reliance on equity and credit holdings to compensate, increasing portfolio risk and the likelihood of contribution pressure if markets weaken.

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Monitoring Report Quarter to 30 June 2026 (Public Version)
findings.headline: Major strategic reallocation underway: exiting active global equity and rebalancing toward fixed income
findings.detail: The fund completed a full exit from Longview Global Equity and partial sales of Dodge & Cox and other active managers, while deploying £295m into UBS Gilts and £330m into Border to Coast credit investments. This significant shift—implemented over one quarter—indicates trustees are concerned about return prospects or the effectiveness of active management in current market conditions.
findings.matters: A pivot toward defensive fixed income positioning suggests the fund trustees expect lower equity returns ahead and are bracing for prolonged underperformance; this reinforces the risk that contributions will be raised to offset shortfalls.
findings.figures: £295m UBS Gilts investment; £330m Border to Coast investment; complete exit of Longview (£301.4m previously)
findings.quote: Full sale of Longview (Active Global Equity), partial sales of Dodge & Cox (Active Global Equity), Osmosis and UBS (Global Passive Equity), along with a cash withdrawal from CBRE Property. £295m investment in UBS Gilts and £330m investment into Border to Coast (IG Credit).

findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Monitoring Report Quarter to 30 June 2026 (Public Version)
findings.headline: Fund has underperformed investment benchmarks consistently over three years, increasing future contribution risk
findings.detail: The fund returned 8.2% per annum over three years against an 11.4% benchmark target, and 8.6% over one year versus 14.1% benchmark. This persistent shortfall across multiple timeframes suggests the fund will struggle to meet actuarial return assumptions, increasing the likelihood of higher employer contributions being required at the next triennial valuation.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are a non-discretionary charge on the council's revenue budget; higher contribution rates directly reduce available resources for service spending and debt servicing, and signal to lenders that financial flexibility is constrained.
