findings.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Monitoring Report Quarter to 30 June 2026 (Public Version)
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level improved to 143% from 132% in one quarter, reducing balance sheet pressure
findings.detail: Assets increased by £219m to £5.5bn and the funding ratio rose 11 percentage points between March and June 2026. This improves the council's stated financial position and reduces immediate contingent liability from the pension scheme. However, the funding level remains 5 percentage points below the 148% recorded at the prior actuarial valuation date (March 2025).
findings.matters: A healthier funding ratio reduces the risk of forced contribution rate increases at the next valuation, which would compress the council's budget and affect its capacity to service debt.
findings.quote: Estimated funding level • 30 June 2026: 143% • 31 March 2026: 132% • 31 March 2025: 148%

findings.headline: This Land Ltd loan restructured March 2025: £59.85m converted to interest-free, fully impaired with MRP spread over 43 years
findings.detail: The £120m loan to council-owned This Land Ltd was restructured in March 2025, split into £60.1m rescheduled at higher interest rate and £59.85m converted to interest-free loan to March 2029. Council took prudent view and fully impaired the £59.85m in 2024/25 accounts. Resulting MRP is spread over 43 years reflecting average remaining life of assets. Public question raised about divergent accounting treatment between council and TLL's own accounts; KPMG content with council treatment.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council's approach to capital impairments on loans to wholly-owned enterprises and use of extended MRP periods to manage cash impact, relevant to governance and capital financing practices.
findings.figures: £59.85m interest-free loan; £60.1m rescheduled at higher rate; 43-year MRP period; £11.85m fair value gain recognised by TLL
findings.quote: In March 2025 the County Council and This Land Ltd (TLL) signed an amendment and re-statement agreement to split TLL's outstanding loan debt into two parts. £60.1m was rescheduled at a higher initial interest rate while £59.85m was converted to an interest-free loan up to March 2029 with no obligation to repay

findings.headline: Solar investments underperforming against expectations driven by cost of borrowing
findings.detail: The committee noted that solar investments are underperforming their expectations due to the cost of borrowing. However, they continue to make a healthy contribution to the council's income. Income expectations will be re-aligned through the budget process.
findings.matters: This signals that the financing cost of council-owned capital investments has deteriorated, reducing expected returns on asset-backed investment strategies.
findings.figures: Underperformance amount not specified
findings.quote: noted that solar investments were underperforming against expectations driven broadly by the cost of borrowing, although they were still making a healthy contribution

findings.headline: 2026/27 small overspend forecast, representing significant improvement from prior year with stronger controls in place
findings.detail: The Head of Finance reported an improved financial outturn flowing into the current year. A small overspend is currently forecast for 2026/27, but this represents significant improvement compared to the prior year. Stronger controls are now in place.
findings.matters: Improving budget control from larger to smaller overspends shows tightening management, though continued overspending in the context of secured three-year funding suggests underlying budget pressure.
findings.figures: Small overspend amount not quantified
findings.quote: A small overspend was currently forecast for 2026/27, but this was significantly less than had been seen in the previous year and stronger controls were now in place

findings.headline: Audit actions: long-overdue items increased from 15 to 21; high-risk actions also increased
findings.detail: While overall outstanding audit actions fell from 87 to 65, the trend on long-overdue items deteriorated. Actions outstanding over a year increased from 15 to 21, high-risk actions also increased, and some resolution dates repeatedly slip. The committee has power to refer non-compliance to service committees.
findings.matters: Growing numbers of overdue and high-risk audit actions suggest control weaknesses are not being remedied, indicating either remediation complexity was underestimated or fixes have been deprioritized.
findings.figures: 15 to 21 actions over one year overdue; 87 down to 65 total outstanding
findings.quote: they highlighted that the number of actions which had been outstanding for more than a year had increased from 15 to 21 and the number of high risk actions had also increased

findings.headline: 2025/26 accounts will not receive unmodified external audit opinion; target return to clean sign-off in 2028
findings.detail: KPMG is building back assurance but the 2025/26 accounts will not achieve an unmodified opinion due to national backstops affecting timely financial reporting. KPMG hopes to move to a modified opinion this year, but reserves and property, plant and equipment require further attention. Target for unmodified opinion is year ending March 2028.
findings.matters: An unmodified opinion is the standard clean audit sign-off; two-year deferral to 2028 indicates unresolved audit issues and suggests governance or accounting complexity.
findings.figures: Target year ending March 2028
findings.quote: The 2025/26 accounts would not receive an unmodified external audit opinion due to the continuing work needed to restore timely financial reporting in local government following the national backstops set by Government

findings.headline: DSG deficit at £96.3m, up over 50% from prior year
findings.detail: The dedicated schools grant reserve deficit increased significantly and the council identified it as a continuing long-term risk through March 2028. Government has announced a grant payment of up to 90% of accrued costs to end of 2025/26, but the timescale is unclear. The deficit continues to accrue due to statutory spending obligations.
findings.matters: A 50%+ year-on-year increase in SEND deficits signals accelerating structural pressure; dependency on government grant relief with uncertain timing creates a cash planning risk.
findings.figures: £96.3m (increase of over 50%)
findings.quote: noted that the DSG total unusable reserve deficit stood at £96.3m at year end which was an increase of over 50% from the previous year

findings.headline: The council has received extensive adverse Ombudsman findings, predominantly concerning delays and failures in special educational needs assessments and education provision.
findings.detail: Appendix 1 lists numerous Ombudsman adverse findings, predominantly in Children, Education and Families services. The complaints centre on delays in EHC Plan assessments, delays in issuing final plans, and failures to provide educational support while assessments are underway. The council has been found at fault in the majority of cases and is making substantial compensation payments ranging from £100 to over £4,800 per case.
findings.matters: Systemic failures in a major service area create direct financial exposure through compensation and indicate management capacity issues affecting service resilience.
findings.figures: Compensation payments documented from £100 to £4,800+ per case; over 40 adverse findings listed
findings.quote: The Council was at fault. As a result Ms X had to wait longer than she should have for a decision on Y's EHC needs assessment and Y had missed education.

findings.headline: Financial reserves have been adjusted to reflect increased risk on loans to This Land, a council-owned shareholding company.
findings.detail: The council holds loans to This Land, a company in which it is shareholder. The Statutory Officers meet weekly to monitor the company. The council has amended financial reserves to reflect elevated risk and reports it continues to review loan strength.
findings.matters: This indicates the council has recognized deterioration in a significant financial asset and increased provisions against loan loss, directly affecting financial resilience.
findings.figures: Loan amounts and reserve adjustment figures not specified
findings.quote: The Council continues to review the strength of loans to This Land, although the financial reserves were amended to reflect a greater risk.

findings.headline: The council was prosecuted by the Health & Safety Executive for deaths on the Guided Busway and has made arrangements to pay a fine.
findings.detail: In 2024/25 Cambridgeshire faced HSE prosecution relating to deaths on the guided busway route, resulting in a fine for which it has made payment arrangements. The Statutory Officers continue to meet weekly to monitor busway safety.
findings.matters: This represents a recognized financial liability and demonstrates a control failure of sufficient severity to trigger criminal prosecution, both material to a lender assessing governance and risk.
findings.figures: Amount of fine not specified in the report
findings.quote: In 2024/25 Cambridgeshire County Council was prosecuted by the Health & Safety Executive in relation to deaths on the guided busway route. This resulted in a fine, which the Council has made arrangements to pay.

findings.headline: Traffic signal infrastructure now at or beyond design life with rising obsolescence costs and global supply chain pressures
findings.detail: Traffic signal assets average 14.3 years old against a design life of 15 years. The strategy identifies 'global decline in availability of halogen lamps, increasing demand to upgrade sites to energy-efficient LED technology, and the growing challenge of maintaining outdated signal control equipment due to obsolescence'. The council is attempting to extend life to 20 years to defer replacement.
findings.matters: Assets now at or past design life with mounting obsolescence create uncontrolled replacement demand. Artificial life extension increases failure risk. This asset category will require significant capital spending as forced replacement occurs.
findings.figures: Average stock age: 14.30 years; design life: 15 years; 192 signalised junctions, 228 light-controlled crossings; replacement cost £47 million
findings.quote: The actual design life of signals infrastructure is 15 years; however, we look to maintain to a 20-year life to sweat the maximum lifecycle from this asset.

findings.headline: Structures assets held in 'Fair' condition accepting moderate risk to public safety as a financial constraint
findings.detail: The council's strategy is to maintain structural assets (bridges, underpasses, retaining walls valued at £444 million) in 'Fair' condition on average. The strategy describes this category as having 'some bridges representing a moderate risk to public safety unless mitigation measures are put in place'.
findings.matters: Accepting moderate public safety risk due to funding constraints creates liability exposure and reputational risk. This represents a deliberate trade-off of safety for affordability.
findings.figures: Structures asset value: £444 million (as at July 2025); 1,200 road bridges, 2,200 public rights of way bridges, 85 other structures
findings.quote: Our average investment per year over ten years means the authority will be able to follow a worst first approach to managing structures countywide whilst keeping the average structural condition, (BSClav), in the 'Fair' condition category.

findings.headline: Multiple significant asset inventory gaps prevent accurate financial planning and mask the true cost of asset management
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges incomplete data for key assets. Drainage inventory collection is noted as 'significant cost'. Highway tree inventory is incomplete with the council noting 'we need to complete a full asset inventory of all our highway trees and risk assess them'. Multiple drainage asset categories are marked 'To be confirmed'.
findings.matters: Incomplete asset data prevents accurate financial forecasting and creates risk that the £57.967m annual requirement is understated. The council cannot confidently manage assets it has not inventoried, and future costs could be materially higher.
findings.figures: 325,000 highway trees on incomplete basis; 60,000+ gullies plus 20% assumed additional gullies; linear drainage unmapped
findings.quote: To complete this we need to complete a full asset inventory of all our highway trees and risk assess them to implement a routine inspection regime.

findings.headline: Population forecast to grow 18% over 19 years, increasing highway demand at a time when maintenance budgets are already insufficient
findings.detail: The council's population is forecast to increase by 18% over the next 19 years. The strategy acknowledges this will require ensuring 'the road network and other highway infrastructure will satisfy the increased potential demand', but the funding envelope is already constrained.
findings.matters: Population growth increases demand on highway infrastructure at a time when maintenance budgets are already insufficient to maintain current asset condition. This compounds the structural funding gap and defers the problem to future administrations.
findings.figures: Population increase forecast: 18% over 19 years
findings.quote: Population in the county is forecast to increase by 18% over the next 19 years (Cambridgeshire Insight - population estimates). In order to satisfy this, there will be a need to ensure that the road network and other highway infrastructure will satisfy the increased potential demand.

findings.headline: Heavy goods vehicle traffic on Cambridgeshire's main roads is 3.7 times the national average, accelerating wear on infrastructure designed for lower loadings
findings.detail: The council reports that HGV traffic density on trunk 'A' roads is 3.7 times the national average, and 56% above average on non-trunk main roads. This traffic composition 'is a major factor that influences the rate at which the highway network deteriorates', creating above-average wear on infrastructure designed for national-average loadings.
findings.matters: Above-average traffic loading accelerates asset deterioration and increases maintenance costs, but the council cannot control this demand-side pressure. This represents a structural cost disadvantage versus councils with lower HGV density.
findings.figures: Trunk A roads: 3.7x national average HGV density; non-trunk main roads: 56% above national average
findings.quote: Traffic Growth in the county is monitored regularly and shows that the density of HGV traffic on Cambridgeshire's trunk 'A' roads is 3.7 times the national average, and on non-trunk main roads it is 56% above the national average.

findings.headline: 40% of Cambridgeshire's road network sits on peat-based soils experiencing accelerated deterioration from climate change
findings.detail: Around 40% of the entire road network lies on Soil Affected Roads (SARs) where 'Climate change and unpredictable weather patterns can have a significant impact on these routes, resulting in excessive and accelerated deformation.' Fenland district is 93% affected. The council is deploying permanent traffic management including lane closures and warning signs in response.
findings.matters: Climate-driven deterioration of soil-affected roads represents an escalating, uncontrollable cost pressure. The council cannot prevent this deterioration through standard maintenance, requiring capital reconstruction and operational constraints. This is an unfunded demand that will grow.
findings.figures: 40% of network affected; Fenland 93% affected, East Cambridgeshire 28%
findings.quote: Around 40% of Cambridgeshire's entire road network lies on peat-based soils. These soils naturally saturate and expand in wet weather and dry out and contract in dry weather. Climate change and unpredictable weather patterns can have a significant impact on these routes, resulting in excessive and accelerated deformation.

findings.headline: Deteriorating road condition across lower-classification roads, with 8% of the cumulative network now in poor ('Red') condition and deterioration accelerating downwards
findings.detail: Carriageway condition data shows asset health declining by road classification. Unclassified roads show only 59% in good condition with 31% in moderate condition and 10% in poor condition. Across all road types, 8% are now in 'Red' condition requiring imminent intervention. The strategy's baseline investment scenario will not improve this; maintenance is reactive only.
findings.matters: Deteriorating road condition increases maintenance costs exponentially (the strategy notes that repair costs for worst-condition assets are 'seven times as costly'). Assets slipping into Red condition require emergency spending, consuming capital budgets and increasing reactive maintenance costs.
findings.figures: Unclassified Roads: 59% Green, 31% Amber, 10% Red; cumulative network: 64% Green, 28% Amber, 8% Red
findings.quote: Unclassified Roads 59% 31% 10%

findings.headline: Annual highway maintenance funding likely to fall short of the £57.967 million required to maintain assets in their current state
findings.detail: The strategy identifies a baseline 10-year investment requirement of £57,967,000 per year to maintain all highway assets in their current condition. However, the council explicitly states that actual spending 'is subject to both the amount of funding provided by national government and its own financial circumstances'. The authority notes it will 'have to prioritise where it invests the funding it has available', indicating a structural funding gap between need and available resources.
findings.matters: A council unable to maintain highways at current condition levels faces deteriorating asset values, escalating reactive costs, and service delivery risk. For lenders, this signals long-term pressure on the council's capital position and future borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Required annual budget: £57,967,000; current funding level not specified in document
findings.quote: It is important to note that the actual amount which the County Council can invest each year is subject to both the amount of funding provided by national government and its own financial circumstances. It is therefore likely that the authority will have to prioritise where it invests the funding it has available to maximise the return on investment.

findings.headline: Cambridgeshire has an £800m road maintenance backlog despite record investment since 2024-25
findings.detail: Despite record levels of highways maintenance funding since 2024-25 (reaching over £78m by March 2026, including government funding of £31.3m), the council has acknowledged an £800m road maintenance backlog resulting from chronic historic national underfunding. The strategy recognizes that sustained investment and changes in approach are required over the long term to address this.
findings.matters: An £800m unfunded backlog represents a significant deferred capital liability that will require sustained future spending and signals substantial historical underinvestment in infrastructure that could affect both the council's asset quality and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: £800m road maintenance backlog, over £78m investment by March 2026, government funding £31.3m
findings.quote: despite sustained record levels of funding put into highways maintenance since the start of 2024-25, the historic and chronic national underfunding for highways by successive Governments has resulted in an £800m road maintenance backlog for Cambridgeshire and it is recognised that sustained investment and changes in approach are required over the long term

findings.headline: 40% of Cambridgeshire's road network is built on peat soil with repair funding requirements the council cannot meet
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly identifies that 40% of the council's network is built on peat soils, requiring repair and maintenance funding levels beyond what is available. Although some funding is allocated in the Capital Maintenance Programme, the council will continue to lobby government to increase highways maintenance allocation to reflect these specific geographic network challenges affecting the north and east of the county.
findings.matters: A council's inability to fund maintenance of 40% of its highway network signals an ongoing structural cost pressure and a geographically-specific liability that affects its financial capacity and may require either additional borrowing or diversion of resources from other services
findings.figures: 40% of the council's network is built on peat soils
findings.quote: 40% of the council's network is built on peat soils, with associated cracking and repairs requiring funding levels beyond what is available. Although some funding is allocated in the Capital Maintenance Programme, safe and appropriate management of these roads is key and the council will continue to make the case to government to increase the highways maintenance allocation

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: HSE prosecution for deaths on Guided Busway project with fine imposed and ongoing safety oversight required
findings.detail: Cambridgeshire County Council was prosecuted by the Health & Safety Executive for deaths on the guided busway route. The council has made arrangements to pay the fine (amount not disclosed). A full safety review was undertaken and members advised of proposed remedial actions. The Statutory Officers continue to meet to oversee the safety regime, indicating ongoing governance concern.
findings.matters: HSE prosecutions indicate serious failures in project governance, safety management, or contractor oversight. Beyond reputational damage and the direct fine cost, it raises questions about the council's capability to manage complex infrastructure projects and whether similar control weaknesses exist in other major projects.
findings.figures: Fine amount not disclosed; involves multiple deaths on public infrastructure
findings.quote: Cambridgeshire County Council was prosecuted by the Health & Safety Executive (HSE) in relation to the deaths on the guided busway route. This resulted in a fine, which the Council has made arrangements to pay.

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation from two-tier to single-tier unitary structure presents significant operational and financial transition risk; implementation decision expected July 2026
findings.detail: Cambridgeshire is undergoing mandatory local government reorganisation, transitioning from a county + seven district structure to single-tier unitary authority (or authorities). The implementation decision was due July 2026. The council acknowledges this will 'introduce new complexities into the management of services, place considerable pressure on existing Council resources, and require robust risk management to mitigate disruption'. The change requires substantial officer and member time via workstreams, Chief Executives' Group meetings, and a dedicated Change Board.
findings.matters: Large structural reorganisations typically generate significant transition costs, loss of institutional knowledge, service disruptions, and financial uncertainties (asset/liability splitting, TUPE implications, system integration). The uncertainty also constrains the council's ability to plan longer-term capital or service strategies.
findings.figures: No quantified transition costs; involves seven councils in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough; implementation decision timeline July 2026
findings.quote: This period of uncertainty and transition will introduce new complexities into the management of services, place considerable pressure on existing Council resources, and require robust risk management to mitigate disruption

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Waste Disposal PFI contract affordability is being actively assessed as a result of financial pressures
findings.detail: The council discloses that it 'has continued to assess options regarding the provision of its Waste Disposal PFI contract closely for financial consequences and impact to ensure this is affordable'. This language indicates concern that the PFI cost may be unaffordable or that alternative arrangements are being considered. PFI contracts typically have long-term fixed commitments that are inflexible and difficult to exit.
findings.matters: If the Waste PFI contract is unaffordable or trending to unaffordability, the council has limited options: absorb the cost (cash flow pressure), reduce other services, or seek exit/renegotiation (which may be costly). PFI commitments often run 25+ years and represent material annual outflows.
findings.figures: No specific PFI cost figures or affordability gap disclosed
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council has continued to assess options regarding the provision of its Waste Disposal PFI contract closely for financial consequences and impact to ensure this is affordable

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Council is actively reviewing 'the strength of loans' to wholly-owned development company This Land Ltd following 2025 restructuring
findings.detail: Cambridgeshire owns This Land Ltd, a development company. The council and company agreed an updated business plan and financial restructuring in March 2025. The report states the council 'continues to review the strength of loans to This Land Ltd'—language indicating concern about loan recoverability or company viability. Board appointments were strengthened in 2025-26, and regular reporting to a Shareholder Sub-Committee is now in place. The core concern appears to be financial underperformance relative to original expectations.
findings.matters: Council-owned development companies have been a source of significant losses for multiple councils (e.g. Croydon, Slough, Thurrock). The phrase 'reviewing the strength of loans' is a red flag indicating management believes there is risk that loans may not be fully recoverable. This could require a material write-down on the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: No specific loan values or accumulated losses disclosed; restructuring and board changes in 2025-26 suggest prior performance shortfall
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there has been regular reporting to the Shareholder Sub-Committee to oversee delivery by the company of their business plan and the council continues to review the strength of loans to This Land Ltd

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit opinion downgraded to 'moderate assurance' with control weaknesses present; implementation of agreed audit actions fell to 66% from 75% in prior years
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit gave a 'moderate assurance' opinion for 2025-26, indicating that audit work has identified control weaknesses presenting medium risk to the control environment. Despite 219 audit actions being due for implementation (fewer than the prior year's 269), only 66% were completed—a decline from 75% implementation in both 2024-25 and 2023-24. One 'essential' recommendation from 2023-24 remains outstanding. Control weaknesses span contract management (identified as 'higher risk'), health and safety (post-HSE investigation), and project/programme governance.
findings.matters: A moderate assurance opinion indicates the governance and control framework is not operating effectively. The declining implementation rate of audit recommendations means identified weaknesses are not being remediated, creating accumulating risk. Outstanding essential actions over multiple years suggest capacity or priority issues in management response.
findings.figures: 66% audit action implementation in 2025-26 vs 75% in 2024-25 and 2023-24; no audits identified with 'major' organisational impact but multiple areas with moderate opinions and control weaknesses
findings.quote: it is the Head of Internal Audit's opinion that overall Internal Audit can provide moderate assurance assurance on the overall adequacy and effectiveness of the organisation's framework of governance, risk management and control within Cambridgeshire County Council for the financial year ended 31st March 2026

findings.paper_title: Item 8 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit accumulated to £96.3m with £33.4m overspend in 2025-26 alone, described as 'perhaps the most significant financial risk to the council'
findings.detail: The council's accumulated DSG deficit reached £96.3m by 31 March 2026, with £33.4m overspent in the single year of 2025-26 alone. The deficit is ringfenced and treated as an unusable reserve; the council cannot use general resources to fund it. Government announced it would fund 90% of the accumulated deficit (by 31 March 2026) subject to conditions, but this leaves a 10% residual (approximately £9.6m) plus further projected overspends post-April 2026 unresolved. The council is pursuing an Inclusion for All strategy and SEND Reform Plan with the NHS.
findings.matters: A £96m+ ringfenced deficit is unsustainable and effectively locks the council out of that capacity for any other use. The trajectory—£33m/year—and source (high-needs special education provision) indicates structural demand that is growing beyond available funding and service capacity constraints. This is precisely the kind of financial distress that concerns lenders.
findings.figures: £96.3m accumulated deficit at 31 March 2026; £33.4m overspend in 2025-26; government to fund 90% of pre-March 2026 deficit subject to conditions and completion of SEND Reform Plan
findings.quote: the 10% residual deficit pre March 2026 and our projections for further expenditure and overspend projected from April 2026 continue to represent perhaps they most significant financial risk to the council

findings.headline: Court of Protection related debt increased £831k, reflecting systemic delays outside council control
findings.detail: Cases requiring Court of Protection involvement grew by £831k (18%). These are particularly complex due to inherent delays in the Court of Protection process itself and complexities supporting individuals under its remit, making resolution inherently unpredictable.
findings.matters: This represents a class of debt where recovery is structurally delayed by external judicial processes; it reduces predictability of cash collection timings.
findings.figures: £831k increase (18% growth in this debt category)
findings.quote: Court of Protection related debt has seen an increase of £831k (18%) demonstrating delays with the Court of Protection process and complexities for individuals needing support in this category.

findings.headline: Long-aged debt (365+ days) increased £3.24m, driven by backdated charges now proving difficult to collect
findings.detail: Debt aged 365–730 days increased by £2.14m and debt over 730 days increased by £1.1m. These increases result from backdated charges stemming from the 2024/25 financial assessment backlog. The council notes these invoices are inherently complex to resolve, with slower recovery rates due to disputes, affordability challenges, and service user engagement issues.
findings.matters: Long-aged debt is increasingly unlikely to be collected; concentration of problematic cases suggests systemic weaknesses in early intervention and billing timeliness.
findings.figures: 365–730 days up £2.14m; 730+ days up £1.1m
findings.quote: Debt within the age bracket 365-730 days has increased by £2.14m and debt over 730 days has increased by £1.1m. These debt brackets have been impacted by the back dated charges rolling into this age profile.

findings.headline: Overall collection rate dropped 12 percentage points year-on-year to 85%, signalling system-wide collection challenges
findings.detail: The council's collection performance for 2025/26 year-to-date is 85% against 97% in the prior financial year. This 12-point deterioration spans all major debt types: Sundry fell from 99% to 87%, ASC from 89% to 74%, creating a system-wide collection efficiency problem.
findings.matters: A sharp deterioration in collection efficiency affects cash flow timing, borrowing requirements, and signals operational challenges in the income management function.
findings.figures: Overall 85% vs 97% prior year; Sundry 87% vs 99%; ASC 74% vs 89%
findings.quote: Collection rates for 2025/26 year to date shows that 85% of all revenue billed has been collected. Collection rates for debt types are Sundry is 87%, Adult Social Care is 74% and NHS is 89%.

findings.headline: Doubtful debt provision increased £1.7m to £9.4m, charged directly to the general fund
findings.detail: The council's doubtful debt reserve rose from £7.7m to £9.4m. This provision is recalculated annually and reflects the council's own assessment that a portion of outstanding debts will never be collected. Movements in this provision are charged to the Income and Expenditure account, directly reducing reported financial position.
findings.matters: An increasing doubtful debt provision signals deteriorating asset quality and reduces the general fund position; it indicates management's own assessment that the council is less likely to collect what it has billed.
findings.figures: Provision increased from £7.7m to £9.4m (£1.7m increase)
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the provision stands at £9.4m, an increase of £1.7m from the previous year, driven by an ageing and growing debt profile.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt increased £3.9m to £24.79m with collection rate falling from 89% to 74%
findings.detail: ASC client contribution debt rose from £20.895m to £24.795m over 12 months (18.7% increase). More critically, the collection rate for 2025/26 fell to 74% from 89% in 2024/25. Overdue ASC debt now represents 39.57% of ASC revenue billed, up 4.76 percentage points year-on-year.
findings.matters: This is the core service delivery and revenue stream for social care; deteriorating collection directly affects cashflow and the council's ability to fund care provision without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £24.79m debt (up from £20.895m), 74% collection rate (down from 89%), 39.57% overdue vs revenue
findings.quote: ASC aged debt is currently £24.79m, an increase of £3.9m compared to twelve months ago. ASC overdue debt percentage versus revenue raised is at 39.57%, which is 4.76 percentage points worse than this time last year.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Appendix A - DSG Deficits and SEND Reforms - March 2026
findings.headline: EHCP assessment backlog creating unfunded support costs in mainstream schools with statutory non-compliance risk
findings.detail: Assessment backlog and poor 20-week performance means schools must support children at SEN Support phase while awaiting EHCP completion (when EHCP is likely to be necessary). Council notes delays are exacerbating school budget pressures and could lead to statutory non-compliance for the LA. Council is developing ad-hoc interim funding formula to address.
findings.matters: Reveals capacity problem in SEND assessment function; creates unfunded cost pass-through to schools; creates compliance and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Cambridgeshire EHCP prevalence 5.9% vs national 5.3%
findings.quote: The delays caused by this situation are having a negative impact on schools and their ability to fully support C&YP , including exacerbating budget pressures within schools. The delays could also lead to statutory non-compliance for the LA.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Appendix A - DSG Deficits and SEND Reforms - March 2026
findings.headline: Government deficit support mechanism ends 2027-28; future funding approach relies on 'departmental expenditure limits' with no guarantee of additional funding
findings.detail: Statutory override for DSG deficits remains in place until end of 2027-28. For 2026-27 and 2027-28, government states LAs 'can expect an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited.' After 2027-28, government intends to meet SEND spend from overall departmental expenditure limits, not from dedicated deficit support.
findings.matters: Creates cliff-edge risk: current deficit support is temporary; council will lose formal deficit funding mechanism by 2029, forcing difficult choices about service provision or reserves.
findings.figures: Statutory override ends 2027-28; HNSG support ends same date
findings.quote: For deficits that arise in 2026–27 and 2027–28, MHLCG have stated that local authorities can expect that they will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited. The statutory override will remain in place until the end of 2027-28…after which the Government intend to meet SEND spend from overall departmental expenditure limits

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Appendix A - DSG Deficits and SEND Reforms - March 2026
findings.headline: High Needs Block funding allocation shows 0% uplift for 2026-27 despite inflation and rising demand
findings.detail: HNB allocations for 2026-27 include no increase for inflation or demand pressures; only changes are due to baselining of grants. This is a flat-cash position while forecast expenditure rises to £184m, creating the £60m+ overspend gap noted above.
findings.matters: Lack of indexation forces prioritization within constrained budgets; signals government is not matching funding to demand, forcing council into deficit management rather than balanced budget provision.
findings.figures: 0% increase in HNB allocation; £184m forecast spend
findings.quote: Current HNB allocations for 2026-27 do not include uplifts for inflation or demand, so 0% increase (only change is due to baselining of grants currently funded directly, so no change in spending power).

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Appendix A - DSG Deficits and SEND Reforms - March 2026
findings.headline: 2026-27 cumulative deficit of £70m projected despite £92m+ government support, council explicitly states this position 'is not sustainable'
findings.detail: High Needs Stability Grant will provide up to 90% of deficit support; LA covers remaining 10%. Even assuming HNSG allocation of circa £92m+, revised cumulative deficit projected to be around £70m by end 2026-27. Council's own assessment is that this trajectory is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Council's own language that a £70m deficit position is unsustainable signals recognition that structural solutions beyond government grant support will be needed; indicates service-level financial planning uncertainty.
findings.figures: £92m+ HNSG allocation; £70m cumulative deficit projected end 2026-27
findings.quote: Even assuming a HNSG allocation of circa £92m+ would still result in a revised cumulative deficit in the region of £70m at the end of 2026-27…. which is not sustainable….

findings.paper_title: Item 4 Appendix A - DSG Deficits and SEND Reforms - March 2026
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to exceed £101m by end 2025/26, with 2026-27 adding £60m+ more overspend
findings.detail: High Needs Block forecast spend is £158.5m against DfE allocation of £115.4m as of February 2026. Cumulative deficit at end of current year will exceed £101m. For 2026-27, forecast HNB expenditure of £184m against flat-cash allocation creates in-year overspend in excess of £60m.
findings.matters: The council runs a major service at structural deficit requiring ongoing government subsidy; this is a credit-relevant indicator of financial stress in a material service area.
findings.figures: £158.5m spend vs £115.4m allocation (2025/26); £101m+ cumulative deficit; £184m forecast spend for 2026-27 with £60m+ in-year gap
findings.quote: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to be in excess of £101m at the end of 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025-26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Private equity and infrastructure holdings of £1.017 billion carry valuation uncertainty of ±23.1%, potentially ranging £782.5 million to £1.252 billion.
findings.detail: The fund holds £1,017.6 million in private equity and infrastructure investments (excluding Cambridge and Counties Bank). These illiquid assets are valued at fair value but lack transparent market pricing, creating a potential valuation range of ±23.1%. The sensitivity analysis shows these holdings could reasonably be valued anywhere from £782.5m (23% lower) to £1,252.7m (23% higher).
findings.matters: Large valuation uncertainties in illiquid assets representing ~19% of fund assets create material risk to the reported financial position; actual realisable value on forced liquidation could be significantly lower.
findings.figures: Private equity/infrastructure £1,017.6m at midpoint; potential range £782.5m to £1,252.7m; represents 30.3% of total fund assets that are classified illiquid
findings.quote: Total private equity and infrastructure investments (excluding Cambridge and Counties Bank – see above) at fair value in the financial statements are £1017.6m. There is a risk that this investment may be under or overstated in the accounts. Note 18 gives a price sensitivity of Alternative investments of 23.1%, which indicates that other private equity and infrastructure values may range from £782.5m to £1252.7m.

findings.paper_title: Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025-26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Pension liability is highly sensitive to discount rate: a 0.1 percentage point change moves the liability by £66 million.
findings.detail: The accounts disclose that pension liabilities will fluctuate significantly with interest rate movements. A 0.1% decrease in the discount rate assumption would increase the pension liability by approximately £66m. Similarly, a 1-year increase in assumed life expectancy would increase the liability by approximately £156m. These sensitivities are material relative to the fund's asset base.
findings.matters: Small shifts in interest rates or mortality assumptions could quickly erase the fund's surplus and force material increases in employer contributions; the council has limited control over these external factors.
findings.figures: 0.1% decrease in discount rate = £66m increase in liability; 0.1% increase in earnings inflation = £2m increase; 1-year increase in life expectancy = £156m increase
findings.quote: For instance, a 0.1% decrease in the discount rate assumption would result in an increase in the pension liability by approximately £66m. A 0.1% increase in assumed earnings inflation would increase the value of liabilities by approximately £2m, and a 1-year increase in assumed life expectancy would increase the liability by approximately £156m.

findings.paper_title: Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025-26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level dropped 15 percentage points to 132% in one year despite investment gains of £345.8 million.
findings.detail: The Fund's actuarial funding level was 147% at the 31 March 2025 valuation but had declined to 132% by 31 March 2026, even though the fund generated a 6.6% annual investment return and assets grew to £5.25 billion. The document attributes this decline to 'changes in actuarial assumptions, including a higher discount rate, rather than underlying asset performance,' suggesting the liability side of the equation grew faster than assets.
findings.matters: The council as administering authority will face higher employer contribution rates at the next triennial valuation if funding levels remain depressed; a continuing decline would directly impact the council's budget.
findings.figures: Funding level 147% (31 March 2025) declining to 132% (31 March 2026); fund value increased £345.8 million to £5.25 billion; 2025 valuation showed £1,558 million surplus
findings.quote: The 2025 valuation informs employer contribution rates for the period 2026-27 to 2028-29. As at 31 March 2026, the funding level was 132%, based on updated asset and liability monitoring undertaken between formal actuarial valuations. The reduction primarily reflects changes in actuarial assumptions, including a higher discount rate, rather than underlying asset performance.

findings.paper_title: Urgent Decision taken by the Chief Executive - Integrated Community Equipment Service
findings.headline: Community equipment service market limited to only 3 national providers with one now insolvent
findings.detail: The national market for integrated community equipment services comprises only three providers: NRS (now insolvent), Medequip, and Millbrook. This oligopolistic structure leaves limited alternatives if current provider encounters difficulties. NRS held contracts with 41 local authorities including 21 London boroughs.
findings.matters: Systemic market risk; limited switching options and negotiating leverage if Medequip encounters financial or operational difficulties; future procurement highly constrained
findings.figures: 3 national ICES providers; NRS held 41 LA contracts including 21 London boroughs
findings.quote: The national market for ICES is limited to 3 main providers including NRS, Medequip and Millbrook.

findings.paper_title: Urgent Decision taken by the Chief Executive - Integrated Community Equipment Service
findings.headline: Contract directly awarded under emergency procurement exemption with acknowledged legal challenge risk
findings.detail: Rather than competitive tender, council exercised powers under Procurement Act 2023 Section 41 and Schedule 5 Paragraph 13 to directly award the contract to Medequip on grounds of extreme urgency and unforeseeable circumstances. Legal counsel confirmed threshold is met but acknowledged potential risk of legal challenge due to non-competitive nature of award.
findings.matters: Potential legal challenge could delay service transition further, incur legal costs, and create uncertainty around contract enforceability
findings.figures: 4-year maximum contract term; maximum value £35,035,788
findings.quote: Utilised the Council's powers under Section 41 and Schedule 5, Paragraph 13 of the Procurement Act 2023 to directly award the contract to an alternative provider. This action was justified on the grounds of extreme urgency arising from unforeseeable and unavoidable circumstances, where compliance with standard procurement procedures would risk disruption to a critical statutory service.

findings.paper_title: Urgent Decision taken by the Chief Executive - Integrated Community Equipment Service
findings.headline: Service initially operating at only 30% of normal activity levels with restricted 65-item equipment catalogue versus 600+ items normally available
findings.detail: On 28 July 2025, the new provider mobilised with a minimal equipment catalogue of 65 items deemed critical for urgent needs (hospital discharge, end-of-life care). By end September 2025, service had reached only 30% of normal activity. The original service delivered over 100,000 items annually with 600+ equipment lines and 14 technicians daily. This represents significant service degradation during transition.
findings.matters: Council unable to meet full statutory obligations under Care Act 2014 and NHS Act 2022 during transition; vulnerable populations receiving restricted support; potential legal challenge risk from service users
findings.figures: 65 items of 600+ normal catalogue (11%); 30% activity level by end September 2025; normal service delivered 100,000+ items annually from single warehouse with 14 technicians daily
findings.quote: On commencement of the contract on 28th July 2025, the incoming provider mobilised their service to deliver a smaller catalogue of 65 items of equipment deemed by health and social care operational specialists to meet the most urgent and critical needs across the community. As at the end of September 2025, the service has reached 30% of normal activity levels.

findings.paper_title: Urgent Decision taken by the Chief Executive - Integrated Community Equipment Service
findings.headline: Previous provider Nottingham Rehab Limited unable to continue operating beyond July 2025 due to serious financial challenges
findings.detail: In June 2025, NRS advised all 41 commissioning authorities of inability to continue without substantial support including inflationary increases and changes to payment terms. Council terminated contract under insolvency clause and activated emergency procurement to direct-award to alternative provider Medequip on 28 July 2025.
findings.matters: Demonstrates systemic risk in adult social care service delivery; indicates market fragility with only 3 national providers and one now insolvent
findings.figures: 41 total commissioning authorities affected; NRS unable to continue beyond end July 2025
findings.quote: In June 2025, NRS advised all commissioning authorities that they faced serious financial challenges that required urgent resolution to enable them to continue to operate. They advised that without this support they could not continue to operate beyond the end of July 2025.
