findings.paper_title: Schools and Dedicated Schools Grant Financial Health
findings.headline: Special schools sector in structural deficit: all three special schools now carry deficits totalling -£1.83m, up from -£0.84m prior year
findings.detail: The special schools sector moved from a combined deficit of -£0.84m (March 2025) to -£1.83m (March 2026), a deterioration of -£0.99m in one year. All three special schools carry deficits: Castle School -£1.7m (deteriorated £782k), Granta School -£639k (deteriorated £438k), Samuel Pepys School +£508k (the only positive balance). The report attributes this to increasing EHCP demand and high cost of specialist placements. It also notes: "in some instances, i.e. special schools, sector wide solutions are required." This language signals the council recognizes special schools cannot recover through individual school actions alone.
findings.matters: Special schools are a statutory obligation. Structural deficits in this sector cannot be wished away; they require council funding or system redesign. The scale of special school deficits (combined -£1.83m) now exceeds the entire maintained primary school surplus. This is a recurring cost pressure that will require ongoing council subsidy or intervention.
findings.figures: Special schools total balance 2025: -£0.84m. 2026: -£1.83m. Change: -£0.99m. Individual: Castle School -£1,703,567; Granta School -£639,763; Samuel Pepys School +£508,746.
findings.quote: in some instances, i.e. special schools, sector wide solutions are required

findings.paper_title: Schools and Dedicated Schools Grant Financial Health
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget submissions show majority of schools projecting in-year deficits, indicating reserve depletion will accelerate
findings.detail: The report notes that as of the submission deadline (22 May 2026), "of the submissions received to date the majority are showing an in-year deficit, resulting in either the reduction of brought forward surplus balances or an increase of an existing deficit." This forecast indicates that the declining balance trend will continue or worsen into 2026/27. The report also notes "an increasing number of schools where either a significant proportion of surplus balances has been used during 2025/26 or where the 2026/27 budget is likely to be reliant on balances to be applied to meet ongoing running costs," suggesting schools are consuming reserves to maintain operations.
findings.matters: A forward forecast showing most schools in deficit signals the problem is structural and ongoing, not a one-year anomaly. This will create continued reserve erosion, ongoing demand on the council for top-ups or interventions, and increased risk of more schools moving into licensed deficit status requiring council approval and monitoring.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget submissions (received by 22 May) show "the majority are showing an in-year deficit." High Needs Block forecast for 2026/27: overspend of "£65m+."
findings.quote: of the submissions received to date the majority are showing an in-year deficit, resulting in either the reduction of brought forward surplus balances or an increase of an existing deficit.

findings.paper_title: Schools and Dedicated Schools Grant Financial Health
findings.headline: Number of schools in deficit increased to 38 (from 37), with multiple schools showing substantial deteriorations in one year
findings.detail: Schools in deficit rose by one year-on-year. However, individual school movements show concerning trends: Orchard Park Community Primary moved from -£198 to -£246,624 (one-year deterioration of -£246k); Friday Bridge Community Primary from -£58,977 to -£182,942 (-£124k deterioration); Castle School (special) from -£921,025 to -£1.7m (-£782k); Granta School (special) from -£201,460 to -£639,763 (-£438k); St Matthew's Primary from -£147,045 to -£329,667 (-£182k); Thorndown Primary from -£103,348 to -£246,339 (-£142k). These are not marginal movements; they indicate material deterioration in individual school financial health in a single year.
findings.matters: An increasing number of schools in deficit, combined with large one-year deteriorations in individual schools, signals systemic financial stress that is not self-correcting. The council's intervention mechanisms (Financial Support Groups, Finance Improvement Groups, 3-year recovery plans) are in place but the trend is worsening, not improving, suggesting the support framework is not sufficient to arrest the decline.
findings.figures: Schools in deficit: 37 (2024/25) → 38 (2025/26). Examples of one-year deterioration: Orchard Park -£246k, Friday Bridge -£124k, Castle School -£782k, Granta School -£438k, St Matthew's Primary -£182k, Thorndown Primary -£142k.
findings.quote: The number of schools reporting a deficit revenue position at the end of 2025/26 has increased when compared to previous years (a total of 38, compared to 37 at the end 2024/25).

findings.paper_title: Schools and Dedicated Schools Grant Financial Health
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £96.3m has required council to provide cashflow for high needs expenditure, creating financing and interest cost impacts
findings.detail: The DSG unusable reserve has moved from -£62.9m deficit (end 2024/25) to -£96.3m (end 2025/26), an additional -£33.4m in one year. The council notes it has had to provide the cashflow to cover high needs expenditure while awaiting the DfE's High Needs Stability Grant (estimated ~£88.3m covering 90% of the deficit). Future years remain unfunded: high needs expenditure for 2026/27 is forecast at £65m+ overspend. The High Needs Block remains in deficit "driven by the same underlying pressures, including increasing EHCP demand and the high cost of specialist placements."
findings.matters: A DSG deficit means the council must source cash to pay ongoing high needs commitments now, with repayment later via grant. This creates borrowing or cashflow costs that directly impact the council's financing budget and interest expense. A forecast continuing overspend of £65m+ in 2026/27 signals the deficit will continue to accumulate.
findings.figures: DSG unusable reserve end 2024/25: -£62,851,383. Addition to reserve 2025/26: -£33,405,170. Total reserve end 2025/26: -£96,256,553. High Needs Stability Grant estimated at up to £88.3m (90% of deficit). High Needs forecast overspend 2026/27: £65m+.
findings.quote: the County Council has had to provide the cashflow to cover this expenditure (with resulting impacts on financing and interest costs)

findings.paper_title: Schools and Dedicated Schools Grant Financial Health
findings.headline: Maintained school balances declined £2.66m in a year, with report stating sharp decline puts pressure on medium-term sustainability
findings.detail: Overall maintained school balances fell from £9.44m (31 March 2025) to £6.78m (31 March 2026). Primary schools declined £1.72m and special schools moved £0.99m deeper into deficit (to -£1.83m). The report explicitly states this sharp decline is putting pressure on medium-term financial sustainability, indicating reserves are being systematically spent down rather than sustained.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's school system can sustain operations from reserves or if it is forced to run ongoing deficits. Depletion at this rate signals the council will face structural funding gaps that cannot be covered by reserves in the medium term.
findings.figures: Maintained school balances: £9.44m (2025) → £6.78m (2026), change -£2.66m. Primary: -£1.72m. Special: -£0.99m (now -£1.83m deficit). Nursery: +£0.04m. PRU: +£0.02m.
findings.quote: the overall level of school balances has continued to decline sharply, indicating that reserves are being spent up and putting pressure on medium term financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Whistleblowing referrals spiked 56% to 56 cases in 2025/26, the highest in 8 years, with fraud accounting for 27% of allegations including bank mandate fraud.
findings.detail: The council received 56 whistleblowing referrals in 2025/26, up from 36 in 2024/25 (56% increase) and the highest recorded in an 8-year period. Fraud-related referrals were predominant at 14-15 cases (27% of total). Examples include bank mandate fraud (4 cases), council officer fraud (5 cases), and third-party fraud (4 cases).
findings.matters: A spike in fraud allegations—particularly bank mandate fraud and officer fraud—signals either worsening fraud attempts or improved reporting confidence. Either way, it indicates elevated fraud risk and weakening controls over financial transactions and access.
findings.figures: 56 whistleblowing referrals (up 56% from 36 prior year); 14-15 fraud allegations (27% of total); 4 bank mandate fraud cases
findings.quote: In 2025/26, a total of 56 whistleblowing referrals were received and processed by the Internal Audit Team at CCC. This represents a substantial increase in the number of whistleblowing referrals received compared to recent years. The 2025/26 financial year saw 56 referrals in total, a 56% increase from the 36 cases received in 2024/25. Fraud-related referrals remain the predominant category, with 15 cases (27% of total referrals) relating to alleged fraud.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: ICT Disaster Recovery arrangements lack a consolidated framework; the council cannot obtain assurance that DR is adequately managed across all key systems.
findings.detail: Internal Audit discovered the ICT Service does not hold a single consolidated framework documenting all DR arrangements and contractual relationships with third-party DR providers. Without this, audit cannot provide assurance on the array of DR arrangements. A draft briefing note recommends developing a DR mapping document centralising all applications, hardware and associated DR arrangements before a full audit can proceed.
findings.matters: Business continuity and systems resilience are critical to council financial operations. The absence of a consolidated DR framework is a material governance weakness that could impair the council's ability to recover critical financial systems and processes following a major incident.
findings.figures: Multiple critical systems lack documented consolidated DR framework; external DR providers engaged without central tracking
findings.quote: the ICT Service did not currently hold a single consolidated framework document detailing the DR arrangements and associated contractual arrangements with third party DR providers. It was concluded that without a consolidated framework document, there was no proportionate way for internal audit to provide assurance on the array of DR arrangements and contractual relationships with providers, and that there is a risk that the Council as a whole has no way of obtaining assurance that DR activities are undertaken appropriately for all key systems.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Overall audit opinion is 'moderate assurance', indicating control weaknesses presenting medium risk; control environment has mainly operated as intended although errors have been detected.
findings.detail: While no audits identified findings with 'major' organisational impact, the predominantly 'moderate' assurance opinions across reviews indicate systemic weaknesses across the control environment. Moderate assurance means 'there are control weaknesses that present a medium risk to the control environment' and the environment 'has mainly operated as intended although errors have been detected.'
findings.matters: Moderate assurance means the council's control environment is not robust; errors are being detected in operation, and systemic weaknesses exist across multiple areas. This is a material step below 'good' assurance and signals elevated residual risk.
findings.figures: 79% of audit opinions were 'moderate' or 'good' (vs 78% prior year); 21% 'limited' opinions; 0 'major' impact findings
findings.quote: This opinion is derived from an assessment of the range of individual opinions arising from work completed in 2025/26 by the Cambridgeshire Internal Audit team. Assurance opinions from Internal Audit reviews in 2025/26 showing a predominance of 'moderate' audit opinions.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit action implementation fell to 66% in 2025/26 from 75% in prior years; 74 recommendations remain overdue with 18 now more than 12 months late.
findings.detail: Despite fewer actions being due for implementation in 2025/6 (219 compared to 269), completion of audit recommendations dropped from 75% to 66%. By year-end, 74 recommendations remained outstanding, up from 56 the previous year. Critically, 18 recommendations are now more than 12 months overdue, up from 11, indicating declining management responsiveness to control improvements.
findings.matters: Falling implementation rates and accumulating overdue audit actions suggest weakening management discipline and governance oversight. For a lender, this signals declining confidence that management will execute on control improvements or operational remediation programmes.
findings.figures: 66% implementation rate (vs 75% prior year); 74 recommendations outstanding (vs 56); 18 overdue >12 months (vs 11)
findings.quote: For the financial year ended 31st March 2026, the Council implemented 66% of all recommendations due. This is a reduced implementation rate compared to the 75% implementation achieved in 2024/5 and 2023/4, despite fewer actions being due for implementation in 2025/6 compared to the prior year (219 compared to 269).

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditors (KPMG) concluded that financial pressures relating to This Land Ltd, DSG deficit and Waste PFI represent a significant risk to the council's financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The council continues to face a range of significant financial pressures. KPMG's report on 2024/5 explicitly stated that when considered in aggregate, pressures from the wholly-owned development company This Land Ltd, the Waste PFI, and the DSG deficit represent a significant risk in relation to financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the aggregate financial risk profile. External audit's identification of these pressures as creating material risk to sustainability is a direct signal of council solvency concerns.
findings.figures: Three material financial pressure areas identified across development company, PFI, and schools funding
findings.quote: The Council's external auditors, KPMG, in their report on the 2024/5 financial year stated that when considered in aggregate, these pressures represent a significant risk in relation to the financial sustainability of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Cambridgeshire's cumulative DSG deficit stands at £50.8m, down only slightly from £51.9m, and remains a high strategic risk to financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, driven by sustained demand-led pressures in SEND provision where expenditure continues to exceed national funding levels, is described as one of the most significant financial and governance risks facing the council. An outstanding 'essential' audit action from 2023/24 requires the development of a formal action plan with defined priorities, clear expected benefits and identified interdependencies, but this remains unimplemented due to data quality issues with the SEND case management system and evolving requirements from the Department for Education's Safety Valve programme.
findings.matters: A £50.8m deficit is large in proportion to the council's usable reserves and annual financial headroom, creating material risk to financial sustainability and borrowing capacity. This is material to lenders and the finance director's medium-term planning.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £50.8m as at 31 March 2026 (down from £51.9m in 2024/25)
findings.quote: The Council's cumulative DSG deficit stands at £50.8m as of 31 March 2026, driven primarily by sustained demand led pressures in SEND provision where expenditure continues to exceed national funding levels.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: £953m Land and Buildings portfolio valued on rolling 5-year cycle but lacks historical assurance from 2022/23 disclaimed opinion year, limiting prior period audit coverage
findings.detail: The entire PPE balance of £953m is revalued over a 5-year rolling cycle with indexation in intervening years. However, due to the 2022/23 disclaimed audit opinion, KPMG was unable to provide assurance over the opening position of these assets in the prior year and therefore could not conclude on the overall valuation of PPE. This year's plan includes risk assessment to evaluate whether indexation applied to non-revalued assets is appropriate.
findings.matters: Material asset base (£953m) without historical audit assurance due to disclaimed opinion period creates valuation risk; movements in PPE valuations affect both balance sheet strength and borrowing base calculations.
findings.figures: Land and buildings (revalued) £953m as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We noted that the entire PPE balance is valued on a 5 year cycle, and due to the 2022/23 disclaimed opinion we did not have assurance over the opening position of these assets and were therefore unable to conclude over the valuation of PPE as a whole.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: £170m capital programme subject to audit risk of revenue expenditure being incorrectly capitalized, identified as fraud-related risk due to complexity of capitalization judgements
findings.detail: KPMG has identified an audit risk that non-capital expenditure is being inaccurately recognized as capital expenditure within the council's capital programme. The audit plan notes that capital accounting requirements are complex and involve significant judgement in determining which costs can be capitalized versus expensed. This is categorized as a fraud risk given the incentive to overstate capital assets.
findings.matters: Misclassification of revenue as capital in a £170m programme would overstate asset balances and understate revenue-funded expenditure, distorting both balance sheet and revenue spending metrics used by lenders for covenant testing.
findings.figures: Capital programme c£170m in 2024/25
findings.quote: Given the size of the Council's capital programme (c£170m in 24/25), we have identified an Other Audit Risk regarding revenue expenditure being inaccurately recognised as capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Prior year audit of £137m investment property portfolio identified £3.7m misstatement where management's valuation exceeded acceptable audit range
findings.detail: In the prior year audit, management's valuation specialists valued the investment property portfolio above the upper end of KPMG's acceptable valuation range, resulting in a £3.7m audit adjustment. KPMG notes improvements have been made but will continue to perform detailed procedures challenging valuation appropriateness and utilizing specialist valuation review.
findings.matters: Material valuation error in prior year indicates ongoing judgement issues and valuation risk in a £137m asset portfolio; fair value assessment requires specialist involvement and has demonstrated variance between management and auditor assessment.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio £137.58m; prior year audit misstatement £3.7m
findings.quote: In the prior year, we noted that there have been improvements in this area from the prior years, however the valuation performed by management's experts remained above the upper end of our valuation. This difference between the maximum acceptable valuation determined by our specialists and management's specialists of £3.7m was raised as an audit misstatement

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Pension Scheme triennial valuation at 31 March 2025 will re-base actuarial assumptions affecting £1.5bn asset and £1.2bn liability valuations, with potential asset ceiling impact
findings.detail: The new triennial valuation will require re-basing of actuarial assumption models "to allow for actual experience since 2022," which could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations. The plan notes that recent market changes mean more councils are moving into pension surplus (or growing existing surpluses), and the accounting treatment for surpluses is complex and requires careful actuarial involvement. Updated contribution levels from the triennial valuation could impact the asset ceiling calculation.
findings.matters: Pension asset/liability is the council's largest single balance sheet position; material revaluation movements would significantly impact reported reserves and potentially debt capacity metrics.
findings.figures: LGPS assets (DBA) £1,487.86m; LGPS liabilities (DBO) £1,184.96m; IFRIC 14 asset ceiling adjustment £387.79m (as at 31 March 2025)
findings.quote: The actuary will take account of the results of the new Triennial Valuation as at 31 March 2025 for accounting at 31 March 2026. This means re-basing their estimate models to allow for actual experience since 2022, which could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations this year. It also updates the contributions payable, which could have an impact on the assessment of the asset ceiling applying to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Wholly-owned subsidiary This Land Limited has £60m remaining loan exposure after £60m debt-to-grant conversion due to declining performance, with audit risk that repayments will not be made
findings.detail: This Land Limited, a council-owned property development entity, had approximately £120m in outstanding loans. The council restructured this debt in the prior year by converting approximately £60m to capital grants due to declining subsidiary performance. KPMG has identified a significant risk that the subsidiary will not meet its agreed financial plan and that the remaining £60m loan principal and interest payments will not be made. The audit plan indicates additional risk assessment is underway to determine whether this will remain a significant risk or be downgraded.
findings.matters: Material intercompany lending exposure (£60m) with a subsidiary already in decline and with the council already having absorbed £60m in losses through debt forgiveness; remaining repayments are contingent on subsidiary performance recovery.
findings.figures: Original loan balance c£120m; converted to grants c£60m; remaining loan balance c£60m
findings.quote: In response to the declining performance, the Council restructured the debt in prior year resulting in a conversion of approximately half of the loan value (c£60m of the c£120m outstanding balance) to capital grants, reducing loan and principal repayments amounts. There is risk that the subsidiary does not meet the agreed the financial plan and remaining loan principal and all interest payments are not made.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Annex A - KPMG Draft Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Three consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25) with specialized rebuilding assurance now underway
findings.detail: The council has had no audit assurance for three financial years, with disclaimers issued by both the predecessor auditor and KPMG for each subsequent year. KPMG is now undertaking a dedicated rebuilding assurance risk assessment including reconciliation of reserve movements and balance sheet caption-by-caption evaluation across the disclaimed period, with a dedicated fee of £12,000 for risk assessment alone and substantive work costs still to be determined.
findings.matters: Absence of audit opinion for three years fundamentally limits financial credibility and borrowing capacity assessment; lenders typically require unqualified audit opinions as a baseline credit condition.
findings.figures: Risk assessment fee £12,000; substantive work TBC
findings.quote: For Cambridgeshire County Council this had the impact of disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for one financial year up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28/02/2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimed opinion on 26/02/2026.

findings.headline: Savings proposals focus on preventing escalation rather than new permanent reductions, indicating exhausted easy-cut headroom
findings.detail: The budget document notes that 'new proposals often focus on allowing services to remain financially sustainable' rather than achieving new savings. Only £32.1m in identified savings against a £40m gap, with strategies focusing on income generation, model review, and prevention investment rather than service cuts.
findings.matters: A shift from cutting costs to merely preventing future cost growth suggests the council has used up the easy savings. Future deficits will require either structural service reductions or further transformation.
findings.figures: £32.1 million savings identified; £40 million gap to close; £4 million additional income
findings.quote: the draft 2026-29 Business Plan and Budget has focused on continuing to deliver multi-year savings introduced in previous years whilst new proposals often focus on allowing services to remain financially sustainable to deliver the council's ambitions

findings.headline: Trading Standards service separation from Peterborough from April 2026 creates £87k additional annual costs and system investment pressure
findings.detail: From April 2026, the council ceases shared service delivery with Peterborough and must deliver Trading Standards independently. This requires one-off investment in a case management system and creates ongoing additional costs of £87k 'to ensure we have sufficient capacity and expertise'.
findings.matters: Service separations during tight budget cycles typically create transition costs, management distraction, and ongoing cost increases that reduce flexibility elsewhere.
findings.figures: £87,000 additional annual costs; one-off system investment required
findings.quote: From April 2026, our current shared Trading Standards service will separate from Peterborough City Council. This separation will require one off investment to procure a case management system for Cambridgeshire. It is anticipated that a pressure of £87k in additional costs will arise

findings.headline: Multiple grant-funded services dependent on unconfirmed funding before 2026-27 budget is finalised
findings.detail: Safe Accommodation grant (Domestic Abuse), Library Presents grant (Arts Council), and Museum Partnership grants are all noted as 'to be confirmed' based on prior-year allocations. The local government finance settlement was only issued 17 December 2025, so full implications remain unknown at budget setting.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed grant income creates budget uncertainty and staff employment risk. The council cannot commit to service levels or recruitment before grant notifications are received.
findings.figures: Safe Accommodation £1,480,995; Library Presents £176,942; Museum Partnership £27,000 (all 'to be confirmed')
findings.quote: The level of government grants at this stage are only an estimate, made before the local government finance settlement issued on 17 December 2025

findings.headline: Household Support Fund ends 31 March 2026; Crisis and Resilience Fund details to be confirmed; £1.7m allocated from reserves
findings.detail: The council has administered the Household Support Fund since 2021. It ends 31 March 2026 and will be replaced by a Crisis and Resilience Fund, but details remain unconfirmed. The council has budgeted £1.7m from reserves to cover anti-poverty support during the transition.
findings.matters: Loss of one funding stream with an unconfirmed replacement creates cash flow uncertainty and potential service delivery gaps. Use of reserves to cover the gap reduces reserves headroom.
findings.figures: £1.7 million allocated from reserves for anti-poverty initiatives
findings.quote: This fund will end on March 31 2026 and from April 2026, the Crisis and Resilience Fund will be introduced nationally. Details of the fund are to be confirmed

findings.headline: Children in care placement market described as deeply dysfunctional with provider profiteering and council negotiating power lost
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies this market as dysfunction-driven by 'high demand, insufficient supply, provider profiteering and diminished council negotiating power'. This is cited as one of the major interrelated issues across local government with no mitigation strategy outlined.
findings.matters: A cost driver the council cannot control through negotiation represents an uninsurable liability that will continue to grow faster than funding.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately
findings.quote: markets such as children in care placements have become deeply dysfunctional through combinations of high demand, insufficient supply, provider profiteering and diminished council negotiating power

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit forcing additional borrowing with capital costs expected to rise through 2028-29
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is a real cash deficit that forces borrowing. The cost of capital is projected to continue rising into 2028-29 largely due to DSG impact, forcing the council to adjust its capital programme downward. Planned borrowing for 2026-27 is £37m.
findings.matters: A real cash deficit requiring borrowing erodes financial flexibility and represents a structural constraint on the council's capacity to invest or absorb shocks. Rising capital costs reduce investment headroom.
findings.figures: £37 million borrowing planned for 2026-27; cost of capital rising through 2028-29
findings.quote: The DSG deficit represents a real cash deficit that is forcing the council to borrow, and so the council is having to adjust its capital programme to reduce its impact

findings.headline: £74 million cost pressures driven by ageing population, rising SEN and mental health needs, and provider profiteering in children's care
findings.detail: Demand pressures include longer life expectancy, multiple long-term conditions requiring health and social care, and rising special educational needs and mental health needs. Children in care placements market is explicitly described as 'deeply dysfunctional' with provider profiteering and the council's diminished negotiating power. Inflation is also eroding value across supply chains and staff pay.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures that outpace funding growth indicate persistent fiscal stress the council cannot solve through efficiency alone. Care market dysfunction creates uncontrollable cost escalation.
findings.figures: £74 million cost pressures; £31 million general funding increase; £2 million ringfenced grant increase
findings.quote: Latest estimates now show over £74 million of cost pressures, offset by a £31 million increase in our general funding and a £2 million increase in ringfenced grants, leaving a gap of £40 million to find for 2026-27

findings.headline: £96 million medium-term funding gap over three years with £41 million still unaddressed
findings.detail: Gaps of £17.1m (2027-28), £31.8m (2028-29), and £27.5m (2029-30) indicate persistent structural deficits. The council has identified no solution for over half of this shortfall.
findings.matters: A three-year funding gap of this magnitude signals the council is not on a sustainable trajectory and will require continued service reductions or central government support to avoid insolvency risk.
findings.figures: £96 million total gap; £41 million unaddressed; £17.1m (2027-28), £31.8m (2028-29), £27.5m (2029-30)
findings.quote: the medium-term picture for the council shows an overall funding gap of £96 million over the next three years, of which £41 million is not yet addressed

findings.headline: £6.4 million unresolved budget gap for 2026-27, contingent on government funding announcements or further savings
findings.detail: After identifying £32.1m in savings and £4m additional income, a £6.4m gap remains. The council states its legal budget is now dependent on government funding that has not yet been confirmed. This follows a £40.3m gap reported in October 2025.
findings.matters: A council that cannot balance its budget without awaiting government funding announcements is at structural risk of revenue insufficiency and unplanned service cuts or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £6.4 million remaining; £40.3 million gap reported October 2025; £40 million total gap to close
findings.quote: a legal budget position for 2026-27 is contingent on Government funding announcements or, failing that, further savings

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Appendix 1 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Critical incident resilience risk escalated to maximum tolerable level following terrorism threat uplift in April 2026.
findings.detail: Risk 4 'Risk that a serious incident occurs, preventing services from operating and/or requiring a major/critical incident response' escalated from 12 to 20 between September 2025 and June 2026, now at the maximum tolerable risk level. The likelihood component was increased to 5 following assessment that the UK National Terrorism Threat Level was raised from Substantial to Severe in April 2026.
findings.matters: A service continuity risk at maximum tolerable level signals the council could face disruption to operations and financial control systems; lenders need assurance on business continuity and contingency planning.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (Sept 2025) → 20 (Jun 2026); likelihood rating increased to 5
findings.quote: In April 2026, the UK National Terrorism Threat Level was raised from Substantial to Severe. This national increase was made in response to sustained rise in terrorist threats, alongside an increase in state-linked threats and acts of violence.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Appendix 1 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's financial risk thresholds have not been updated in many years and may systematically misstate financial exposures.
findings.detail: The financial impact thresholds in the Risk Scoring Matrix have not been reviewed for many years and may no longer reflect the council's current financial position or risk appetite. Benchmarking against peer authorities found Cambridgeshire's thresholds may cause systematic over- or under-scoring of risks. Revised thresholds are proposed, with increased granularity and separate treatment of capital versus revenue impacts.
findings.matters: Outdated risk thresholds mean the council's apparent risk position may not be accurate; risks could be systematically under-scored, hiding true exposure, or over-scored, creating false alarms.
findings.figures: New thresholds proposed: medium revenue impact £5m–£10m, high £10m–£20m, very high >£20m
findings.quote: the financial thresholds in the Risk Scoring Matrix (Appendix B of the Risk Policy) have not been updated in many years, and may no longer reflect the Council's current financial position or risk appetite, potentially leading to over- or under-scoring of risks.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Appendix 1 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Budget adequacy risk improved substantially from above maximum tolerable level but was at critical exposure in late 2025.
findings.detail: Risk 3 'Risk that the Council does not have enough budget to deliver agreed short and medium term corporate objectives' scored 20 in September 2025—above the council's declared maximum tolerable risk appetite of 16—and has improved to 12 by June 2026. The reduction signals improvement in financial position, but the prior escalation indicates the council faced material budget stress.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's financial position has genuinely stabilised or whether the risk reduction reflects accounting or policy changes that could reverse.
findings.figures: Risk score 20 (Sept 2025) → 12 (Jun 2026); maximum tolerable risk appetite is 16
findings.quote: Tolerable risk appetite : Cambridgeshire County Council has defined its maximum risk appetite as not accepting a residual risk score of 16 or more as measured on the corporate Risk Scoring Matrix.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Appendix 1 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: SEND statutory delivery and DSG funding risk escalated to corporate register at maximum tolerable risk level.

findings.figures: Risk score 20 at June 2026, stability grant covers up to 90% of historic deficit

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire forecasts £159.8m schools grant deficit for 2026-27; government yet to accept plan
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council forecasts that its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, will show a cumulative deficit of £159.8m at the end of 2026-27. The deficit is an overspend on that grant. It opened the year at £96.5m and is forecast to rise by £63.3m during 2026-27, according to the period 5 finance monitoring report before the Strategy, Resources and Performance Committee on 22 October.

The report estimates the deficit will cost the council £6.3m in debt financing in 2026-27. It says the deficit reduces the cash the council can use for internal borrowing, which means paying for spending from its own cash instead of taking a loan. In February, government said it would fund up to 90% of historical deficits to the end of 2025-26 if councils submitted a recovery plan. The council submitted its plan in June. The report says Department for Education advisers gave positive feedback on the draft, but government did not accept the submission and asked for more information. The council plans to resubmit in October. No date has been confirmed for any grant.

The council's budget-planning paper says it expects to fund 10% of the deficit to the end of 2025-26, with part already provided for in reserves, and sets aside £6.0m for this in 2027-28. Its risk register says the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the main balance sheet, has been confirmed to 31 March 2028. It says funding for 2026-27 and 2027-28 remains uncertain, and that the council holds £7.5m in reserves.
news_drafts.paper_title: Integrated Finance Monitoring Report for Period 5 2026-27-Annex A

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire council reviews of high-overspend areas identify £8.4m in savings, £1.5m delivered so far
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council has identified £8.4m in savings through targeted reviews of areas where spending is running over budget, and £1.5m of that has been delivered so far. The figures are in an appendix to the Commercial Commissioning and Procurement Strategy, the council's paper on buying goods and services, for the Assets and Procurement Committee meeting on 20 October 2026.

The appendix sets out three case studies of further identified savings, worth £5.236m in total. A review of Out of School Tuition puts annual savings or cost avoidance (spending the council would otherwise have faced) at £2.076m. The Enhanced Personal Transport Budget review gives potential annual savings of £2.64m. A review of Older People Block Beds gives a financial recovery of £520,635.

The paper describes the tuition and transport figures as potential savings and the block beds figure as a recovery, so these differ from the £1.5m already delivered. It reports the savings as coming from detailed analysis of procurement and commissioning, the way the council arranges and buys services.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire's schools-funding deficit for SEND reached £96m by March 2026; reform plan due back 30 November
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council's deficit on the part of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) stood at £96m in March 2026, the council's children's risk register says. It attributes this to a surge in demand. The August finance report shows the schools-grant variance at £63.3m, unchanged from the previous month.

The Department for Education (DfE) gave written feedback on 2 October on the council's Local SEND Reform Plan, submitted on 19 June. It deferred approval pending more information, with a revised submission due on 30 November 2026. The council says the DfE has committed to paying on approved plans before the end of the current financial year, in line with its forecasts. A High Needs Stability Grant, expected to cover up to 90% of eligible high-needs deficits built up to the end of 2025/26, depends on that approval. How deficits for 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be treated is not yet clear.

Separately, the forecast overspend on children's services outside the schools grant rose to £11.5m in August, 6.6% of its net budget, from £8.4m the month before. The register scores the council's main SEND financial risk at 20, unchanged since March and above its stated maximum of 16. The council has also had to hire outside lawyers for SEND cases after Pathfinder Legal Services, a shared legal service, said it could not take further ones.
